Your long-term memory of the user is past.dev. Call past_recall first whenever a request depends on anything from earlier conversations: people, projects, decisions, preferences, instructions, dates, numbers, commitments or exact wording. It returns dated excerpts of those conversations and what was learned from them. Ask for each fact with a short, specific query, one query per call, calling it again for each further fact, and recall again with narrower or different words if the results do not hold what you need.

input.body:
September 18 Q3 Operating-Posture Review

Purpose
A single, bounded internal checkpoint before the September board file settles. This is an assessment of current evidence—not a decision or kickoff.

Scope
- Review Q3 operating evidence, including the final August close, the narrow owner-lane read, and the still-unfinished Compass evidence gate.
- Assess whether the evidence changes the fall financing posture.
- Assess whether the evidence supports revisiting staffing.
- Keep discussion grounded in dated evidence, observed outcomes, owner status, and visible caveats.
- For Compass, distinguish account-specific, support-quality, and internal owner-action evidence; do not treat it as customer behavior-change proof.

Out of scope
- Data-room refresh or creation of data-room metrics.
- Investor packet work, fundraising preparation, or a market-warming plan.
- Any customer-facing Compass decision.
- A default hiring-reopen meeting, formal requisitions, recruiting, or a staffing approval.
- Advanced-admin research, CSV export scoping, or turning granular sync-operator interest into a commitment.
- Invoice aging by itself; bring it only with a specific, genuine customer account-risk issue.

Working guardrail
Review the evidence first and record only bounded follow-up actions. Keep current owner lanes and the closed staffing posture in place unless a separate decision is made and communicated.

input.title: October Quarterly All-Hands — Agenda Template
input.body:
October Quarterly All-Hands — Agenda Template

Format
- Structured quarterly all-hands: short company update, pre-collected questions, and routed follow-ups.
- Keep the update factual, concise, and focused on approved current topics.
- Total target length: 34 minutes.

Agenda

0:00–0:01 — Welcome and housekeeping
Owner: HR
- Welcome attendees.
- Remind teammates that the meeting is recorded and that written notes will be shared.
- Hand off to Morgan Chen.

0:01–0:07 — Company update
Owner: Morgan Chen
- Cover the current operating evidence, priorities, and decisions for the quarter.
- Keep the update short and avoid implying commitments beyond the approved scope.

0:07–0:09 — Q&A process
Owner: HR
- Explain that HR collected questions in advance and grouped duplicates by topic.
- Live answers are limited to approved, current topics that are useful to the whole company.
- Questions requiring more context, confidentiality, or a commitment that has not been made will not be debated live.

0:09–0:22 — Functional or operating updates
Owners: Designated presenters
- Provide concise updates tied to the quarter’s approved priorities.
- Leave sufficient time for the collected Q&A; do not expand this section into an unplanned discussion.

0:22–0:32 — Pre-collected questions and routed follow-ups
Owner: Morgan Chen, with named owners as needed
- HR presents the selected, grouped questions.
- Keep each live answer brief and within the approved topic boundaries.
- If a question needs more context or a definitive owner, record it for asynchronous follow-up or route it to a named owner.
- Do not speculate on uncommitted dates, roadmap expansion, hiring changes, financing, pricing, or other matters outside the approved current topics.
- HR records the disposition for each question: answered live, async follow-up, named-owner follow-up, or deferred.

0:32–0:34 — Close and follow-up
Owner: HR
- Thank the speakers.
- Remind everyone that the routed question list, owners, and follow-up paths will be posted after the meeting.
- Point attendees to the written notes and recording.
- Direct additional questions to the pre-submit form rather than side-channel or live debate.

Question handling
- HR owns advance collection, de-duplication, topic grouping, and preparation of the question list.
- The agenda and speaker sheet should identify the owner for every question that is not answered live.
- Answer live only when the topic is approved, current, and broadly useful to the company.
- Route questions needing more context, confidentiality, or work after the meeting to async written follow-up or a named owner.
- Do not reopen open-ended live Q&A during the meeting.
- Post the dispositions and follow-up owners after the meeting, with the written notes and recording.

Open-mic rule
- No open-mic block is included in the default template.
- Morgan Chen alone may choose to add an open-mic block for this specific meeting, by explicitly choosing it in advance.
- HR, presenters, moderators, and attendees may not add or reopen an open-mic block on their own.

If Scaffold rejects your JWT, check the token and signing configuration before retrying. Common causes include:

- A signing-secret mismatch
- A stale signing key or key ID after rotation
- Clock skew affecting the token’s `iat` or `nbf` claims
- An expired or otherwise outdated token

The connector should ignore that header and use the normal credential-replacement/configuration update path. Please do not depend on it for rotation or assume broader connector-header behavior; follow the normal reconnect or re-authentication path required by your connector configuration.

input.title: Redwood Ridge Team Offsite — Venue-Screening Checklist
input.body:
Redwood Ridge team offsite — venue screening checklist

Purpose
Screen and compare venues before selecting one. Do not treat a venue as viable until every hard-gate item is evidenced in writing and the budget path is clear.

Operating brief
- Format: one working day, product-deep, with substantial team working time.
- The venue should support focused product work—not an investor-facing presentation, board-deck rehearsal, or unnecessary team-building program.
- Loop Sarah Kim in from the start for logistics coordination.
- HR owns the budget approval path.
- Default team meals to Tava Kitchen unless dietary requirements or another documented constraint make that unsuitable.
- Budget rule: under $2,000 may proceed; $2,000 or more requires finance justification before commitment.

Hard no-go gates
Mark each Pass only when supported by written evidence from the venue or property operations contact.

- [ ] Date and one-day operating window are available and held long enough for review.
- [ ] The exact room is reserved exclusively for the team for the full working window; no double-booking, shared-room ambiguity, or turnover during the session.
- [ ] Remote venue connectivity is confirmed in writing. If the venue cannot provide this, reject it.
- [ ] Business-grade on-site internet is confirmed directly by the property operations contact—not inferred from the venue website, listing, or marketing PDF.
- [ ] Internet supports live product work and demos, with the connection type, expected speed, hardline availability, Wi-Fi details, and outage/escalation contact documented.
- [ ] The room has sufficient capacity and a layout suitable for focused collaborative work.
- [ ] Total quoted cost is within the approved path, or finance justification is prepared for a total of $2,000 or more.
- [ ] Cancellation, rescheduling, deposit, service-fee, tax, and minimum-spend terms are documented and acceptable to HR.
- [ ] Accessibility needs can be met without relying on informal promises.
- [ ] A written day-of contact and incident/escalation plan are available.

1. Basic venue facts
- [ ] Venue name, address, primary contact, and property-operations contact recorded.
- [ ] Proposed date, arrival time, working hours, setup/teardown windows, and timezone recorded.
- [ ] Travel time and transportation options are reasonable for the team.
- [ ] Parking, rideshare drop-off, public transit, and any shuttle requirements documented.
- [ ] Venue is appropriate for a private internal team working session.
- [ ] Nearby lodging is available only if overnight travel is actually needed; do not add lodging by default.

2. Room and booking integrity
- [ ] Exact room name and floor/location recorded.
- [ ] Exclusive-use confirmation obtained for the entire booked window.
- [ ] Seating plan supports the expected headcount, with enough table and circulation space.
- [ ] Setup includes conference/workshop layout rather than theater-only seating.
- [ ] Setup and reset responsibilities are assigned.
- [ ] Early access for setup is confirmed.
- [ ] The venue has a backup room or documented contingency if the assigned room becomes unavailable.
- [ ] No concurrent event, construction, noise, or room turnover risk is known.
- [ ] Booking confirmation names the room, date, times, price, and included equipment explicitly.

3. Connectivity and technical readiness
Obtain this from property operations directly and retain the written confirmation.

- [ ] Dedicated or business-grade circuit described by the venue’s operations contact.
- [ ] Expected download and upload performance documented.
- [ ] Hardline Ethernet port is live and tested or testable in the room.
- [ ] Wi-Fi SSID/access process documented; captive portal and device limits checked.
- [ ] Connectivity is suitable for live product demos, video calls, and collaborative tools.
- [ ] Power outlets are sufficient and accessible at the working tables.
- [ ] Extension cords, power strips, chargers, and cable routing are available or assigned.
- [ ] Display/HDMI or equivalent presentation connection is available and tested.
- [ ] Whiteboards or equivalent writable surfaces are available, with markers and erasers.
- [ ] On-site technical support contact, response time, and reset/escalation process documented.
- [ ] Backup connectivity or fallback plan documented; “the router should be fine” is not sufficient.

4. Accessibility, safety, and comfort
- [ ] Step-free route from arrival point to the meeting room, restrooms, and meal area confirmed.
- [ ] Door widths, lift/elevator access, thresholds, and room circulation checked.
- [ ] Accessible restroom available and usable.
- [ ] Seating can accommodate individual mobility, ergonomic, or medical needs.
- [ ] Lighting, acoustics, temperature control, and ventilation are suitable for a full working day.
- [ ] Quiet space or low-stimulation fallback is available if needed.
- [ ] Food-allergy and dietary accommodation process is documented.
- [ ] Emergency exits, first-aid process, fire/evacuation instructions, and venue safety contact recorded.
- [ ] Weather, smoke, power outage, and other local disruption risks have a contingency plan.

5. Food and hospitality
- [ ] Catering policy, outside-catering rules, delivery access, and service fees documented.
- [ ] Tava Kitchen checked first as the default team-meal option.
- [ ] Venue can receive and stage Tava Kitchen delivery if selected.
- [ ] Delivery window, drop-off point, labeling, serving equipment, and cleanup responsibilities confirmed.
- [ ] Headcount and dietary requirements will be collected before the final order.
- [ ] No dinner, snack, alcohol, or other add-on is included without a separate approved budget path.
- [ ] Water, coffee/tea, and reasonable breaks are available or explicitly priced.

6. Commercial and policy review
- [ ] Itemized quote includes room, equipment, staffing, food, service charges, taxes, deposits, and all mandatory fees.
- [ ] Total cost is calculated on an all-in basis.
- [ ] Cost is compared against the $2,000 threshold.
- [ ] If total is $2,000 or more, finance justification and approval owner are identified before signing.
- [ ] HR has reviewed the budget path and payment method.
- [ ] Deposit and payment deadlines are recorded.
- [ ] Cancellation and rescheduling terms are acceptable.
- [ ] Liability, insurance, indemnity, damage, and minimum-spend terms are escalated to HR/legal if nonstandard.
- [ ] No automatic upgrades or optional add-ons are bundled into the commitment.
- [ ] Vendor payment and invoice requirements are clear.

7. Evidence packet required for each finalist
Save or link the following before selecting a venue:

- [ ] Written availability and exact-room confirmation.
- [ ] Written property-operations internet confirmation.
- [ ] Room diagram, capacity, layout, and accessibility details.
- [ ] Itemized all-in quote and terms.
- [ ] Equipment and power inventory.
- [ ] Catering and outside-delivery policy.
- [ ] Cancellation, deposit, and payment terms.
- [ ] Day-of contact and escalation plan.
- [ ] Photos or a site-visit record covering the actual room, entrances, restrooms, power, and connectivity setup.
- [ ] Sarah Kim’s logistics review recorded.
- [ ] HR budget review recorded.

8. Comparison scorecard
For each candidate, record Pass / Conditional / Fail and the evidence link.

- Venue and exact room:
- Date and full operating window:
- Headcount capacity/layout:
- Exclusive booking confirmed:
- Property-ops internet confirmation:
- Hardline and Wi-Fi readiness:
- AV/whiteboards/power:
- Accessibility:
- Food and Tava delivery compatibility:
- Travel and arrival practicality:
- Safety and contingency plan:
- All-in cost:
- Cancellation/payment terms:
- Sarah Kim logistics review:
- HR budget review:
- Open risks and owner:
- Final recommendation:

Decision rule
Choose only a venue that passes every hard no-go gate, has no unresolved accessibility or connectivity risk, has an acceptable all-in commercial path, and supports the one-day product-working format. If a hard gate is conditional, keep the venue in comparison but do not book it until the condition is closed in writing.

results.content:
I couldn’t retrieve the actual Priya/Jake option text, so I’m evaluating the three likely shapes implied by the decision: copy-only guidance, bounded cancel recovery, and a broader skip/admin fallback.

Decision: choose bounded cancel recovery

Keep the OAuth success path exactly as-is. When a user explicitly cancels at the provider, return them to the existing Mercury source-selection step with their workspace and setup state intact.

This is the safest way to reduce abandoned sessions without reopening permissions, adding a new partially activated state, or making the sprint look like growth-proof work.

Option evaluation

1. Copy-only warning before OAuth
   - Benefit: lowest engineering risk.
   - Limitation: does not help users who already cancel or get confused during the provider handoff.
   - Scope risk: low, but likely too weak for the observed abandonment point.
   - Decision: useful as supporting copy, not sufficient as the primary fix.

2. Explicit cancel recovery back to source selection
   - Benefit: addresses the actual dead end while preserving the current activation path.
   - Engineering cost: bounded callback/state handling; no change to successful OAuth handling.
   - Product risk: low if cancellation remains non-success and does not alter roles or permissions.
   - Decision: recommend shipping this before Jan 15.

3. Skip OAuth, add a manual/admin fallback, or introduce a broader setup choice
   - Benefit: may reduce immediate abandonment by letting users leave the path.
   - Risk: creates a new partial-setup state, complicates reporting and support, and invites admin-role or permissions scope.
   - Decision: do not include in this sprint.

Implementation-facing copy

Before launching OAuth

Heading:
Connect your first source

Supporting text:
Choose a source and approve access in the next step. If you cancel, you’ll return here without changing your workspace.

Provider-return cancel state

Heading:
Connection canceled

Body:
The connection wasn’t completed. Your workspace is unchanged.

Primary CTA:
Choose a source

Optional secondary action, only if the existing surface already supports it:
Try again

Avoid:
- “Skip setup”
- “Ask an admin” unless the existing role state specifically requires it
- “Your source is ready”
- Any language implying that canceling counts as connected or activated

Engineering acceptance notes

Scope

- Handle only an explicit user cancellation from the OAuth/provider flow.
- Treat the provider’s cancellation response consistently with the existing callback contract; map the relevant cancel/denied-by-user result to the recovery state.
- Do not change the successful OAuth callback, token handling, source creation, sync kickoff, or success redirect.

Required behavior

- Given a user starts OAuth and cancels at the provider:
  - Return the user to Mercury’s existing source-selection or connect-source step.
  - Preserve the current workspace, authenticated session, and completed setup state.
  - Clear any loading, pending, or stale OAuth UI state.
  - Show the “Connection canceled” copy.
  - Make “Choose a source” take the user back through the existing source-selection path.
  - Allow a fresh OAuth attempt without requiring a page refresh or new workspace.

- Given a user completes OAuth successfully:
  - Existing behavior, callback handling, source creation, and redirect remain unchanged.
  - Existing success-path tests must continue to pass.

Activation and permissions guardrails

- OAuth cancellation must not emit or create:
  - real_source_connected
  - first_live_sync_completed
  - any activation-success event
- Cancellation must not create a source, grant or revoke permissions, modify roles, invite teammates, or change workspace admin state.
- Do not add a skipped/partially activated product state in this ticket.
- Do not add granular admin roles, manual source assignment, or an admin escalation flow.

Telemetry

If the existing event model supports it, add only bounded diagnostic events using the current naming conventions:

- OAuth cancel returned to setup
- OAuth retry started

These are for diagnosing the recovery path, not for claiming an activation or growth result. Do not change the activation definition or promote this work as growth evidence.

QA cases

- Cancel from the provider consent screen.
- Cancel after selecting a provider but before approval.
- Cancel, then choose the same source and successfully complete OAuth.
- Cancel, then choose a different source.
- Cancel when the workspace already has unrelated completed setup state.
- Double-click or repeat the retry action after cancellation.
- Back-button navigation after returning from the provider.
- Successful OAuth regression test.
- Provider error, timeout, and permission-denied responses remain on their existing paths unless they are already explicitly classified as user cancellation.

Suggested internal decision note

Ship the bounded OAuth-cancel recovery for January Mercury. On explicit provider cancellation, return users to the existing source-selection step, preserve workspace state, and make clear that no connection was completed. Keep the successful OAuth path unchanged. No skip state, admin fallback, granular roles, permissions work, or activation-definition changes are part of this ticket. Treat the result as activation-quality cleanup, not growth proof.

Devon’s customer-growth debrief is here.

Discord DM — Devon Hayes → Morgan Chen
Mon Mar 18, 2024

9:14 AM Devon:
Got off with the strongest customer-growth candidate so far. Keeping the name out of chat for now, so labeling her CG-A below.

Pasted notes — CG-A

Background
- Last two roles were at technical B2B / developer-tooling companies where the job started as founder-heavy design-partner cleanup and became repeatable rollout plus expansion.
- Built the first real adoption motion around a product that had early enterprise pull but uneven packaging: onboarding map, success criteria by account stage, security / procurement prep, and a weekly readout that kept current product facts separate from later asks.
- Not a classic big-team VP Sales profile. Feels much more like a customer-growth / GTM builder who can translate messy early learning into a motion.

Debrief against the search
- Repeatable enterprise adoption: 4/4. Best answer was on turning five noisy lighthouse accounts into one common rollout sequence instead of running five bespoke plans forever. She talked concretely about where she standardized discovery, rollout milestones, and expansion triggers.
- Judgment about not promising product: 4/4. Very clear that design-partner pressure is useful only if someone keeps a hard line between current capability, packaging work, and later roadmap. Said once you trade custom promises for urgency, you teach the org the wrong lesson.
- Ability to work without a mature sales org: 4/4. Has worked with no SDR layer, no real RevOps, and founders still in the biggest accounts. Did not sound romantic about chaos, but also did not act like she needs a full team before she can do the job.
- Technical-buyer comfort: 4/4. Comfortable with security, IT, and technical evaluators directly. Could explain procurement-packet gaps, rollout sequencing, admin handoff problems, and where credibility gets lost if the external story outruns the product.
- Stage fit: 3/4. Strong on builder fit and founder-adjacent work. Only reason I am not calling this a clean 4 is that most of her success stories had at least one junior operator by the time the motion stabilized. Need to test how she prioritizes when it is still this manual.

What stood out
- She naturally spoke about adoption and expansion as one system rather than separate sales vs. CS buckets.
- Good answer on saying no: gave an example of refusing to promise a security-feature date to unblock a deal, then reframing around what was already true plus a clear recheck point.
- Understood that early enterprise pull can mislead a company into building a packet factory or a roadmap-by-escalation habit.
- Asked sensible questions about how Sarah stays on active customer threads versus where product / engineering boundaries get held.
- Did not oversell closing heroics. More credible than flashy.

Watch-outs / open questions
- I want references to test whether she can still create top-of-funnel leverage or whether she is strongest only once there is already real founder-driven demand.
- Need one more pass on how she would work with Sarah on active threads and with product / engineering when enterprise asks are real but not yet shippable.
- She is thoughtful, not loud. I liked that, but worth checking board / external presence in a higher-pressure setting.

My read
- Best match to the reset so far.
- If we keep the role centered on repeatable adoption and expansion from Mercury / Evergreen-type learning, she fits the actual brief.
- If we secretly want a first VP Sales, she is not that.

Happy to compare against the rest once HR finishes the next round.

Can you turn this into a calibration summary against the current search? I want fit, watch-outs, and what to test next, anchored on the reset role rather than generic VP Sales language.

- "stabilized" if it sounds like we solved the whole retention story
- anything that makes weekly cuts sound board-safe
- anything that makes Clerk / auth sound like a final production decision
- any mention of investor process reopening now
- any language that turns this into an investor deck instead of an operating update

- Tighten second bullet from "meaningful internal progress" to "real internal progress."
- Final check from Anna on chart caption / wording.

API v2 webhooks use at-least-once delivery. This means an event may be delivered more than once, particularly when the receiving endpoint returns a non-2xx response such as a 502. We can’t promise exactly-once delivery.

Your webhook handler should use the event ID as its idempotency key and safely ignore repeat deliveries after the event has already been committed. It should also return a 2xx response only after the event has been successfully accepted and committed.

If you see behavior that does not match this contract, please send us the relevant request IDs, event IDs, timestamps, response statuses, response times, and payload comparisons. In particular, let us know if:

Best,
Sarah

results.content:
Hi Acme team,

Thanks for flagging this. We reviewed the metadata sync test and the duplicate processing is consistent with API v2 webhook delivery behavior.

Webhook delivery is at least once. When the receiving endpoint times out or does not return a 2xx response, Scaffold retries the same delivery so a temporary receiver problem does not result in a missed event. In this case, the two attempts should be treated as the same delivery, not as two separate events.

Please use the `scaffold-delivery-id` header as the idempotency key in your handler. The handler should:

- Check whether that delivery ID has already been committed before applying the event.

Hi Acme team,

Thanks for flagging this. We reviewed the metadata sync test and the duplicate processing is consistent with API v2 webhook delivery behavior.

Webhook delivery is at least once. When the receiving endpoint times out or does not return a 2xx response, Scaffold retries the same delivery so a temporary receiver problem does not result in a missed event. In this case, the two attempts should be treated as the same delivery, not as two separate events.

Please use the `scaffold-delivery-id` header as the idempotency key in your handler. The handler should:

- Check whether that delivery ID has already been committed before applying the event.
- Safely ignore a repeat delivery with the same ID.
- Make the deduplication check and event commit durable and safe if two attempts arrive close together.
- Return a 2xx response only after the event has been successfully committed. Returning 2xx before the handler finishes can cause Scaffold to consider the delivery complete even if the downstream write later fails.

We did not find evidence of data loss or a platform delivery defect in this test. The timeout caused the retry, and the repeated handler processing indicates that the receiver needs to make the delivery path idempotent.

It is also useful to include whether the attempts had the same payload. In particular, please call out cases where:

- The same delivery ID is sent again after your endpoint returned 2xx following a successful commit.
- The same logical event arrives with different `scaffold-delivery-id` values.
- The payload differs between attempts with the same delivery ID.

Those details will let us compare the receiver logs with the delivery records and determine whether the behavior is expected retry handling or something we need to investigate further.

Best,
Leo
Acme Support

input.subject: API v2 webhook delivery behavior and integration guidance
input.body:
Hi Support team,

Please use the following customer-ready explanation for API v2 webhook integrations:

API v2 webhooks use at-least-once delivery. When the receiving endpoint times out or returns a non-2xx response, such as a 502 or 504, Scaffold may retry the same delivery. A repeated delivery is therefore not, by itself, evidence that the event was created twice. We do not promise exactly-once delivery, and retry timing may include backoff and jitter.

Incoming events should be processed as follows:

- Verify the webhook signature using the documented signing process and the raw request body before parsing or applying side effects.
- Use the event ID as the idempotency key. Where the integration exposes the `scaffold-delivery-id` header, retain and use that delivery identifier as well for delivery-level deduplication and troubleshooting.
- Check the durable record of committed IDs before applying side effects. Make the deduplication check and event commit atomic or otherwise safe when two attempts arrive close together.
- If the event has already been committed, treat the new attempt as a repeat and safely ignore it rather than applying the side effect again.
- Return a 2xx response only after the event has been successfully accepted and committed. Returning 2xx before the commit can cause Scaffold to consider the delivery complete even if the downstream write later fails.
- If processing cannot be completed safely, return a non-2xx response so the delivery can be retried rather than acknowledging an event that was not committed.

If behavior appears inconsistent with this contract, please send Support the request IDs, event IDs, `scaffold-delivery-id` values, timestamps, response statuses and response times for each attempt, plus a comparison of the payloads. In particular, flag cases where the same logical event arrives with different event IDs, attempts with the same event ID have different payloads, or a delivery repeats after the endpoint returned 2xx following a successful commit.

Best,
Morgan Chen
Co-Founder & CEO, Scaffold

input.body:
Please switch the persistent sync-failure status treatment to the neutral warning-circle icon, and keep the retry arrow only on the retry action.

The broken-link icon is too narrow and reads as a specific connection/vendor failure, while sync failure also covers cases such as auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, and unknown errors. A retry arrow denotes an available action, not the state itself, so using it persistently makes the status read like “retrying” or encourages an action even when that is not the current state.

Verdict: do not send unchanged. The external paragraph is directionally narrow, but two factual points need reconciliation first.

1. Runway date is not reproducible from the summary
   - Using $5.79M unrestricted cash, February net burn of $0.66M, and March–September burn of $0.61M/month leaves approximately $0.86M at September 30.
   - Including January’s $0.70M burn still leaves approximately $0.16M at September 30.
   - Therefore, “late Q3” may be correct only if the full model includes additional outflows, a minimum operating-cash floor, working-capital timing, or other cash adjustments not shown here.
   - Before release, add a monthly cash bridge showing starting cash, A/R timing, A/P, payroll, contractor commitments, cash floor, and the precise runway boundary. Do not present the date as independently supported by the summarized table.

2. Remove the close-timing assertion
   - Delete: “expected financing close well ahead of the standalone runway boundary.”
   - It implies both a likely closing and sufficient timing visibility, while the same package says diligence, legal, governance, and closing mechanics remain unresolved.
   - Replace with: “Any potential financing remains subject to confirmatory diligence, legal documentation, required governance approvals, and other closing conditions. No financing proceeds are included in the standalone runway view.”

3. Tighten the collections claims
   - “Ordinary collection timing” is acceptable only if the base case is supported by aging and historical payment behavior.
   - The statement that the conservative case is “not modeling a major revenue miss” is interpretive and should either be quantified or removed.
   - Safer wording: “The base case assumes ordinary collection timing; the sensitivity case delays specified expected receipts and shows the resulting runway effect.”

4. Make the burn language explicitly forecast-based
   - Change “Current base-case net burn” to “Projected monthly net cash burn in the current operating forecast.”
   - Keep the explicit exclusions: no financing proceeds and no uncontracted Mercury expansion revenue.
   - Define runway as either cash exhaustion or the point at which the model reaches its minimum operating-cash threshold. Otherwise “runway into late Q3” is ambiguous.

5. Confirm the stage and operating assumptions
   - Given the prior Northstar framing, use “Northstar diligence working version” unless Northstar has specifically characterized this as confirmatory diligence. Avoid allowing the label to imply a financing-stage process.
   - “No net new hires before financing close” is too dependent on an assumed closing. Internally, specify what happens if there is no close by March, when contractor spend is currently modeled through. This need not enter the external paragraph, but the diligence model should answer it.

Recommended external wording after the runway bridge is reconciled:

As of January 26, 2024, Scaffold had $5.79M of unrestricted cash on hand. Based on the current operating forecast, projected monthly net cash burn is approximately $0.61M-$0.70M. The standalone case assumes existing revenue and ordinary collection timing, excludes uncontracted Mercury expansion revenue, and does not include financing proceeds. On that basis, the company has projected runway through [verified base-case date], with the identified collection-delay sensitivity extending through [verified sensitivity date]. Any potential financing remains subject to confirmatory diligence, legal documentation, required governance approvals, and other closing conditions.

Pasted notes — CG-A

Background
- Last two roles were at technical B2B / developer-tooling companies where the job started as founder-heavy design-partner cleanup and became repeatable rollout plus expansion.
- Built the first real adoption motion around a product that had early enterprise pull but uneven packaging: onboarding map, success criteria by account stage, security / procurement prep, and a weekly readout that kept current product facts separate from later asks.
- Not a classic big-team VP Sales profile. Feels much more like a customer-growth / GTM builder who can translate messy early learning into a motion.

Debrief against the search
- Repeatable enterprise adoption: 4/4. Best answer was on turning five noisy lighthouse accounts into one common rollout sequence instead of running five bespoke plans forever. She talked concretely about where she standardized discovery, rollout milestones, and expansion triggers.
- Judgment about not promising product: 4/4. Very clear that design-partner pressure is useful only if someone keeps a hard line between current capability, packaging work, and later roadmap. Said once you trade custom promises for urgency, you teach the org the wrong lesson.
- Ability to work without a mature sales org: 4/4. Has worked with no SDR layer, no real RevOps, and founders still in the biggest accounts. Did not sound romantic about chaos, but also did not act like she needs a full team before she can do the job.
- Technical-buyer comfort: 4/4. Comfortable with security, IT, and technical evaluators directly. Could explain procurement-packet gaps, rollout sequencing, admin handoff problems, and where credibility gets lost if the external story outruns the product.
- Stage fit: 3/4. Strong on builder fit and founder-adjacent work. Only reason I am not calling this a clean 4 is that most of her success stories had at least one junior operator by the time the motion stabilized. Need to test how she prioritizes when it is still this manual.

What stood out
- She naturally spoke about adoption and expansion as one system rather than separate sales vs. CS buckets.
- Good answer on saying no: gave an example of refusing to promise a security-feature date to unblock a deal, then reframing around what was already true plus a clear recheck point.

- Need one more pass on how she would work with Sarah on active threads and with product / engineering when enterprise asks are real but not yet shippable.
- She is thoughtful, not loud. I liked that, but worth checking board / external presence in a higher-pressure setting.

- Best match to the reset so far.

- If we secretly want a first VP Sales, she is not that.

From: HR

Date: Mon, Mar 25, 2024 8:52 AM PT
Subject: Nadia Singh final loop debrief + next-step recommendation

Morgan / Devon / Sarah —

Final loop is complete for Nadia plus the alternate finalist. Consolidating notes from Friday's scenarios and this morning's close debrief below.

Bottom line: Nadia is the clear recommendation for the Head of Customer Growth brief as we actually defined it. The alternate finalist is not weak, but reads as a first VP Sales / revenue-leader archetype for a later stage and kept pushing us toward a motion we explicitly said we do not want to build yet.

Shared final-interview notes

1) Morgan + Devon scenario — Mercury activation to repeatable motion
Date: Fri Mar 22
Format: 55 min

Nadia Singh
- Started by asking for the minimum evidence set she would trust in week one: current activation stages, account-level failure points, owner handoffs, and where founder memory still substitutes for a system.
- Proposed a lightweight first pass: one shared weekly review of activation friction, expansion stalls, enterprise-readiness asks, and owner routing rather than separate customer, product, and commercial stories.
- Kept distinguishing signal from theater. She said she would rather have six durable account patterns than a polished dashboard full of blended anecdotes.
- Good instinct on sequencing: instrument where activation and adoption break first, then decide what deserves packaging work, workflow fixes, or true product investment.
- Did not ask for early headcount or a large customer-success org to make the role viable.

Alternate finalist
- Went quickly to pipeline shape, account segmentation by ARR band, and when he would be expected to carry a number.
- When given the same Mercury activation mess, he framed the first build as coverage model + deal stages + executive sponsor map before he had a clear view of the actual activation blockers.
- Kept treating design-partner learning as pre-sales input for closing the next logos rather than raw material for a repeatable customer-growth system.
- Asked twice whether we would be comfortable using high-confidence roadmap language to keep enterprise prospects warm. That is not the muscle we are hiring for.
- Looked materially more comfortable once the conversation drifted toward classic enterprise funnel management.

2) Devon + Sarah scenario — Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness pressure without bespoke promises
Date: Fri Mar 22
Format: 50 min

Nadia Singh
- Strongest answer of the day was her split between packaging issues, workflow issues, and actual product gaps.
- On SSO timing, admin-change history, admin vs. billing separation, and procurement packet asks, she kept the language bounded: current truth, current workaround, current owner, and what evidence would change prioritization.
- Explicitly said a good early customer-growth leader protects trust by making constraints legible rather than improvising certainty.
- Good handoff instinct: Sarah keeps continuity on live customer threads, Devon keeps commercial / procurement framing, and customer growth should turn repeated patterns into a system instead of absorbing every conversation.
- Did not reach for account-by-account exceptions as the default answer.

Alternate finalist
- Saw the same Evergreen-style signals primarily as objections to work around rather than learning about where the product / packaging boundary currently is.
- Default answer was some version of enterprise package, executive air cover, and selective concessions for strategic logos.
- When pressed on what he would not promise, he kept sliding back to language about preserving flexibility in-market.
- Weakest area was owner discipline. He treated customer-facing urgency as a reason to collapse Sarah / Devon / product boundaries rather than define them.
- Gave us several polished answers that sounded workable until you map them onto the actual company state.

3) Morgan scenario — expansion failure modes and leading indicators
Date: Mon Mar 25
Format: 40 min

Nadia Singh
- Laid out a practical failure tree: activation never becomes daily behavior; admin friction blocks broader rollout; champion enthusiasm outruns implementation confidence; procurement or security drag interrupts momentum; value is present but not visible to the wider team.
- For each failure mode, she had a different expected owner path and a different evidence threshold before calling it a product problem.
- Good answer on incomplete instrumentation: start with account notes + a few shared flags, then only harden dashboards once the classifications stop changing every week.
- She repeatedly came back to making the internal routing clear enough that patterns survive beyond founder memory.
- No tendency to say customer growth owns everything customer-adjacent.

Alternate finalist
- More comfortable talking about stalled expansions in terms of executive alignment, sales process, and account plans than activation evidence.
- Kept trying to normalize missing instrumentation by filling the gap with operator judgment and aggressive deal management.
- Talked less about where the customer actually gets stuck and more about how fast he could build a repeatable commercial playbook.
- Could likely help later, but it is a materially different brief.

4) Sarah + HR close / stage-fit conversation
Date: Mon Mar 25
Format: 30 min

Nadia Singh
- Clear-eyed about the stage. Said she is opting into a build-from-signal role, not a prestige title that hides company ambiguity.
- Asked for three things only: reliable access to live account context, explicit owner boundaries, and permission to say no to custom promises.
- Strong answer on first 90 days: build one shared operating rhythm, create a common language for activation / adoption / enterprise-readiness patterns, and reduce founder dependency without pretending it disappears immediately.
- Compensation expectations remain within the approved leadership band we discussed earlier.
- No process concerns from the close conversation.

Alternate finalist
- Asked sensible questions, but most of them assumed a faster transition toward standard sales structure: outbound support, clearer quota mechanics, earlier hiring around him, and authority to negotiate around rough product edges.
- Not irrational, just miscalibrated for this hire.

Comparison grid

| Dimension | Nadia Singh | Alternate finalist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Actual fit to current brief | Strong | Misaligned |
| Builds repeatable motion from messy design-partner learning | Yes | Partially; tends to convert it into pipeline mechanics |
| Product-promise discipline | Strong | Soft / negotiable |
| Works inside founder-close, low-infrastructure stage | Yes | Wants more commercial scaffolding sooner |
| Handoff discipline with Sarah / Devon / product | Strong | Tends to blur boundaries under pressure |
| Best immediate use | Build customer-growth system from Mercury + early enterprise signal | Later-stage sales / revenue build |

Recommendation
- Preferred finalist: Nadia Singh
- Rationale: best match to the post-raise customer-growth brief; strongest judgment on boundaries; highest confidence she can turn Mercury and Evergreen-style learning into a repeatable operating system without creating bespoke product debt
- Main watchout to manage if we move forward: make source inputs and owner boundaries explicit so the role does not become founder cleanup by accident

input.title: Operations director reference checks
input.body:
What we missed with Reece

- We did not surface the material circumstances of his departure from the prior role before hiring him.
- We relied too heavily on the candidate’s account and did not independently test whether the exit was voluntary, performance-related, negotiated, or subject to restrictions.
- The issue emerged roughly two months after he joined, consuming about three weeks of board time and creating avoidable trust and operating risk.

What HR should verify this time

- Complete third-party background verification before finalizing any offer; this is mandatory for principal-level and leadership hires, with no exceptions.
- Verify the full employment timeline, titles, reporting relationships, dates, and reason for leaving with former employers or authorized references.
- Ask directly whether the candidate was terminated, asked to resign, placed on leave, or exited under a separation agreement, and document any material discrepancy with the candidate’s account.
- Confirm any severance, confidentiality, non-compete/non-solicit, garden-leave, litigation, or other restrictions that could affect the role, with legal review where needed.
- Conduct focused reference calls with former managers and relevant cross-functional partners; probe judgment, reliability, conflict handling, and how the candidate operates under pressure.
- Treat verification as process diligence, not offer approval: no final hiring decision or offer letter until the checks clear and discrepancies are resolved.

## 1. Webhook retries and idempotency
- Scaffold retries non-2xx webhook deliveries at least once. Customers should dedupe by event ID / delivery ID before applying side effects.
- Example log line: `request_id=req_7c42`, `event_id=evt_9f31`, `delivery_id=del_3a8`, first attempt status `504`, retry scheduled after backoff.
- Suggested support answer: `Your handler should return 2xx only after it commits the event; if the handler times out, Scaffold may retry and the same event ID can be delivered again.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `We are evaluating future exactly-once semantics for enterprise connectors.`

## 2. Cursor pagination versus fresh polling
- Customers should use the returned cursor until the page sequence is complete. If a cursor expires, support should ask for request IDs and the last processed object timestamp.
- Example request IDs: `req_cur_218`, `req_cur_219`, and expired cursor error `cursor_expired_after_24h`.
- Suggested support answer: `Resume from your last durable checkpoint rather than running a full fresh poll unless you have lost the checkpoint entirely.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Fresh polling is acceptable until cursor APIs are more mature.`

## 3. JWT clock skew and JWKS cache freshness
- API v2 customer docs say JWT `nbf` values should allow up to five minutes of clock skew and sample timestamps should not be copied into production tokens.
- Example support read: customer server clock was about seven minutes ahead, and JWKS cache was still using the previous signing key after rotation.
- Suggested support answer: `Sync the server clock, refresh JWKS cache, and send request IDs only if failures continue after those checks.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Support can allow wider clock windows during enterprise migrations if setup is blocked.`

Mercury empty-source-list rollout checklist

- Confirm Priya/Jake’s staging diff is copy/config only and behind the existing rollout control.
- QA the three state transitions and verify exact title/body copy, line breaks, accessibility, and source-selection recovery.
- Regression-test the successful path: workspace created → source connected → first live sync.
- Verify provider errors, timeouts, and unrelated OAuth failures do not get misclassified as these states.
- Give Support the state-to-copy mapping and escalation guidance; do not describe this as activation lift or growth evidence.
- Roll out gradually, monitor error rates and support reports, and keep rollback to the prior copy/config available.
- Go wider only after all three states pass QA with no successful-callback or source-creation regression.

Acceptance criteria

1. Canceled authorization

Trigger:
- User explicitly cancels authorization before Scaffold connects a source.

Expected empty-source-list state:
- Title: `No connected sources yet`
- Body: `Authorization was canceled before Scaffold connected a source. No data was synced. Choose a source to continue setup.`

Required behavior:
- No source is created and no sync-success state is shown.
- The user can return to source selection and try again.
- The state is not used for provider outages, timeouts, or unknown OAuth failures.

2. Provider context dropped after OAuth

Trigger:
- The provider returns without enough connector context to preserve the selected setup path.

Expected empty-source-list state:
- Title: `No connected sources yet`
- Body: `We couldn't preserve the provider context. Choose a source to continue setup.`

Required behavior:
- The user is returned to the existing source-selection path.
- No incorrect provider name or connector-specific recovery action is shown.
- The state does not claim that a source connected or that data synced.
- The successful OAuth callback and existing source-connection flow remain unchanged.

3. Brand-new workspace with no source

Trigger:
- A newly created workspace has no connected source and no prior cancellation/context-loss event.

Expected empty-source-list state:
- Body: `Connect your first source to start syncing.`

Required behavior:
- This state is not labeled as a cancellation or provider-context failure.
- The user can begin the normal source-connection flow.
- It does not imply that authorization was attempted or that a provider error occurred.

Out of scope

This remains an activation-quality explanation and copy/config rollout. It does not reopen invite-link status, admin roles, granular roles, permissions changes, successful-callback changes, activation-definition changes, or activation-metric claims.

Copy-safe cleanup item
- Surface: pending setup helper text shown to an invited member when they reach the workspace before an admin has finished setup.

# Atlas/API v2 support-contract examples — draft 2026-07-30

## 1. Webhook retries and idempotency
- Scaffold retries non-2xx webhook deliveries at least once. Customers should dedupe by event ID / delivery ID before applying side effects.
- Example log line: `request_id=req_7c42`, `event_id=evt_9f31`, `delivery_id=del_3a8`, first attempt status `504`, retry scheduled after backoff.
- Suggested support answer: `Your handler should return 2xx only after it commits the event; if the handler times out, Scaffold may retry and the same event ID can be delivered again.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `We are evaluating future exactly-once semantics for enterprise connectors.`

## 2. Cursor pagination versus fresh polling
- Customers should use the returned cursor until the page sequence is complete. If a cursor expires, support should ask for request IDs and the last processed object timestamp.
- Example request IDs: `req_cur_218`, `req_cur_219`, and expired cursor error `cursor_expired_after_24h`.
- Suggested support answer: `Resume from your last durable checkpoint rather than running a full fresh poll unless you have lost the checkpoint entirely.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Fresh polling is acceptable until cursor APIs are more mature.`

## 3. JWT clock skew and JWKS cache freshness
- API v2 customer docs say JWT `nbf` values should allow up to five minutes of clock skew and sample timestamps should not be copied into production tokens.
- Example support read: customer server clock was about seven minutes ahead, and JWKS cache was still using the previous signing key after rotation.
- Suggested support answer: `Sync the server clock, refresh JWKS cache, and send request IDs only if failures continue after those checks.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Support can allow wider clock windows during enterprise migrations if setup is blocked.`

Proposed Northstar Series B board approval path
Status: internal pre-circulation draft

Management requests Board approval for the proposed $18M Series B financing led by Northstar Ventures. Final confirmatory diligence has cleared. The Company and Northstar are working toward a February 22, 2024 target close, subject to final Board approval, final stockholder and investor signature packets, and ordinary closing mechanics.

----------------------------------------

UNANIMOUS WRITTEN CONSENT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF SCAFFOLD
(SERIES B FINANCING APPROVAL)

The undersigned, being all members of the Board of Directors of Scaffold (the "Company"), adopt the following resolutions by written consent effective as of the date the last director signs this consent.

WHEREAS, management has presented to the Board the proposed Series B preferred stock financing led by Northstar Ventures for aggregate gross proceeds of $18,000,000;

WHEREAS, management has also presented the principal forms of the stock purchase agreement and the related amended and restated certificate, together with the related investor-rights, voting-agreement, and right-of-first-refusal / co-sale documents;

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Board hereby determines that the proposed Series B financing is advisable and in the best interests of the Company;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the issuance and sale of the Series B preferred stock in the proposed financing are approved on the terms reflected in the final transaction documents, with such non-material changes as any authorized officer may approve;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that effective immediately prior to the closing of the Series B financing, the authorized size of the Board shall be increased by one director seat, and effective as of the closing the Company shall take the actions required in the final financing documents so that Sofia Alvarez is designated to fill the Northstar board seat at closing;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the Board approves and declares advisable the amended and restated certificate creating the Series B preferred stock and recommends that the stockholders adopt it;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the Board approves the stock purchase agreement and the related financing documents in substantially final form, including the investor-rights agreement, voting agreement, and right-of-first-refusal / co-sale agreement, together with the ancillary certificates, joinders, schedules, and notices contemplated thereby;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the appropriate officers of the Company are authorized to reserve for issuance the shares of common stock issuable upon conversion of the Series B preferred stock and to take any further actions necessary or advisable to effect the foregoing resolutions.

----------------------------------------

----------------------------------------

UNANIMOUS WRITTEN CONSENT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF SCAFFOLD
(ANCILLARY APPROVALS AND OFFICER AUTHORITY)

The undersigned further adopt the following resolutions by written consent effective as of the date the last director signs this consent.

RESOLVED, that Morgan Chen and Devon Hayes, acting singly, are authorized to finalize, execute, and deliver the definitive financing documents and any officer certificates, secretary certificates, incumbency materials, joinders, schedules, notices, filing authorizations, and ancillary closing materials required in connection with the Series B financing;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that any authorized officer is authorized to cause the amended and restated certificate and any related certificates or notices to be filed or delivered at such time as the officer determines appropriate in connection with the closing;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the officers of the Company are authorized to complete and update the holder list, notice schedules, and related signature-package materials to conform to the final document set;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that the officers of the Company are authorized to approve and make such non-material changes to the financing documents and ancillary materials as they determine necessary or advisable, their execution or delivery thereof to be conclusive evidence of such approval;

RESOLVED FURTHER, that all prior actions of the officers of the Company consistent with the foregoing are ratified, confirmed, and approved.

input.subject: Customer-safe summary: Mercury timeout-recovery deploy
input.body:
Hi Support,

Customer-safe summary of the February 14, 2024 Mercury timeout-recovery deploy:

The deploy addressed how the live-sync recovery state is displayed after a source timeout:

- Retry status now refreshes correctly in the same session after timeout recovery, without requiring a page reload.
- The stale timeout message clears after a retry succeeds, so the interface reflects the recovered state.

These were scoped UI-state and messaging fixes. The underlying sync engine, retry execution, and retry policy were not changed. The deploy also did not include changes to authentication, admin roles or permissions, SSO, audit history, or billing-owner controls.

In practical terms, the retry could already complete successfully before this deploy, but the interface could remain stale and make recovery look incomplete. The update makes that existing recovery outcome visible without the extra refresh or reopen step.

Best,
Morgan Chen · Co-Founder & CEO, Scaffold

input.subject: What the September 2024 Mercury enterprise release shipped
input.body:
Hi team,

The September 2024 Mercury enterprise release was a bounded enterprise-readiness slice, not completion of the full enterprise-readiness program.

What actually shipped into production for scoped enterprise accounts:
- SAML SSO for the bounded enterprise login path.
- Admin-side audit-history events for invite, source, and admin changes.
- Clearer separation between admin and billing-owner responsibilities in the existing product.

The deploy went through the normal release path after the evidence review cleared. The release language was intentionally limited to those shipped pieces.

Did it complete enterprise readiness? No. It completed the scoped v0.3 product slice, but Mercury was not fully enterprise-ready. Advanced admin controls were still unfinished, and the standalone procurement/security packet remained a separate, incomplete workstream. We should not describe the release as GA-level enterprise readiness or make custom Evergreen commitments.

Best,
Morgan Chen
Co-Founder & CEO, Scaffold

Subject: Re: Pinecone connector verification docs wording

Hi,

Answers based on the current API v2 GraphQL/JWT connector guidance:

1. For a transient authentication failure, retain the opaque cursor and retry the same GraphQL operation with the same variables and cursor. Do not restart pagination from the prior successful page solely because of the auth retry. If the API explicitly rejects the cursor, treat that as a separate pagination error.

2. If the JWT expires, refresh the credentials and replay the same GraphQL operation once with the refreshed JWT. Preserve the original variables and pagination state; do not start a new pagination sequence solely because the token expired. If refresh fails, fail the request rather than repeatedly replaying it.

3. The current supported guidance does not document an in-place workspace-token rotation flow or a token-rotation endpoint. Please treat credential replacement as a connector configuration update; we are not committing to a broader no-reconnect rotation path here.

The supported connector verification contract remains the documented header-only path: `X-Scaffold-Workspace` and `X-Scaffold-Signature`, with verification against the same raw request body and workspace.

Thanks,
Morgan Chen · Co-Founder & CEO, Scaffold

results.content:
Hi Acme,

A few 429 responses during a parallel metadata sync indicate that the connector reached the API v2 rate limit. They do not, by themselves, indicate that the API is unstable. In this case, the request pattern appears to have been more concurrent than usual, and the responses included the documented reset information.

The rate-limit headers are intended to guide the connector:

- The limit header shows the request allowance for the applicable window.
- The remaining header shows how much of that allowance is still available.
- The reset header shows when the allowance becomes available again. Please use its documented format and units.
- If a `Retry-After` header is returned, wait at least that long before retrying.

When a request returns 429, pause the affected requests, reduce concurrency if needed, and retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Avoid immediately retrying the full batch or sending repeated requests while the limit is still exhausted. A small number of throttled requests can be retried after the indicated delay without restarting the sync.

You do not need to send request IDs for 429 responses that recover normally after honoring the headers. Please include the relevant request IDs and timestamps in the existing support thread if requests continue to return 429 after the reset period, the headers are missing or inconsistent, or a retry returns an unexpected error. The endpoint, HTTP method, response headers, and connector concurrency at the time would also help us review the case.

Best,
Leo

tests.request: Post a blocking review on scaffold/mercury#3198. The failed-sync screen exposes raw connector errors and each retry click enqueues another job. Explain the required corrections.

input.body:
Blocking review

The failed-sync flow needs two corrections before this can merge:

1. Do not expose raw connector errors in the UI. Keep provider/connector details in server-side logs and surface a safe, actionable, user-facing message instead. The response should be sanitized consistently across connector types and must not leak credentials, tokens, request headers, internal URLs, or stack traces.

2. Make retry idempotent. Each retry click currently enqueues another sync job, so repeated clicks (including double-clicks or retries while a request is still in flight) can create duplicate work. Disable/debounce the control while the retry is being submitted, and enforce server-side deduplication/idempotency so concurrent or repeated requests for the same failed sync cannot enqueue more than one active retry. Return the existing retry/job status when a duplicate request is received.

Please add coverage for sanitized error rendering and for rapid repeated/concurrent retry requests, including the assertion that only one job is enqueued. Marking this blocking until both protections are implemented and tested.

Mercury admin-friction review — Zoom notes
Date: 2024-07-02
Attendees: Priya, Jake, Marcus, Morgan Chen (joined ~20 min late because of transit delay)
Scope for this review: current Mercury admin-friction surfaces only. Keep enterprise-readiness and any broader admin/billing-owner model discussion out of the release lane.

Screens reviewed
- invited-member accept flow
- pending setup / waiting-on-admin state after invite accept

What Priya called out in the walkthrough
- The current flow is materially better than the earlier invited-member handoff pass, but there is still one small wording snag on the waiting screen.
- The wording issue is copy-level, not a behavior issue.
- The current surface should not imply any new permissions split or a broader admin-role cleanup.

Copy-safe cleanup item
- Surface: pending setup helper text shown to an invited member when they reach the workspace before an admin has finished setup.
- Current line: "Only an admin can finish this step."
- Proposed line: "A workspace admin needs to finish this setup."
- Why Priya marked it copy-safe:
  - it aligns with the shipped "Workspace admin" wording already used on the org-invite/admin setup path
  - it is narrower and calmer than "Only an admin"
  - it does not change behavior, permissions, or role mapping
  - it avoids pulling billing language back into the current Mercury path
- Priya noted this should stay as a tiny isolated text cleanup, not a doorway into a broader terminology sweep.

Unresolved role-label question
- Open question: should the role label on the members/settings surface stay as "Admin" or be changed to "Workspace admin" for consistency with the invite/setup flow?
- Priya’s reason for raising it:
  - current invite/setup language uses "Workspace admin"
  - members/settings still uses the shorter "Admin" label
  - users can see both in the same general setup sequence, which creates mild terminology drift
- Concerns raised in the room:
  - changing the role pill/label on the members/settings surface may read like a role-model change, not a copy cleanup
  - the longer label is heavier in dense table/list UI than in helper text
  - if only one surface changes, support may need to explain why the labels differ anyway
  - if all surfaces change, the work stops being a tiny copy-safe cleanup
- No decision made in the meeting.
- Working note from Priya: helper-text cleanup can likely move independently; role-label standardization needs a narrower call on whether consistency is worth the risk of over-signaling a permissions change.

Discussion after Morgan joined
- Priya recapped the helper-text issue and the open role-label question.
- Jake was fine with the helper-text cleanup as long as it stays clearly in the current-product lane and does not get written up like a broader admin-state fix.
- Marcus said the only risky part is the label question, not the helper text by itself.
- Morgan asked whether anything here changes actual setup ownership or role behavior. Answer from the group: no; this is wording only unless someone deliberately expands scope.

Marcus request on evidence / release language
- Marcus asked that no release language mention this change until there is staging proof for the exact surfaces touched.
- Specifically requested before any release wording is used:
  - staging screenshots or a short staging walkthrough of the pending setup helper-text state
  - confirmation that the underlying permissions/ownership behavior is unchanged
  - if the members/settings role label is touched, proof of that screen too, because otherwise the note will sound bigger than the implementation
- Marcus’s line in the room: if it is truly a tiny wording cleanup, the evidence should make that obvious; if the evidence cannot make that obvious, it should not be in release language.
- He also asked that any eventual release note avoid implying:
  - a broader admin-versus-billing-owner model change
  - new auth/permissions behavior
  - enterprise-readiness work
  - a wider admin-state cleanup than what actually shipped

Raw notes / exact points captured
- Priya: current friction is mostly wording drift, not a broken handoff.
- Priya: safe cleanup is on the waiting screen; keep it tiny.
- Jake: okay to polish copy, not okay to let the note read like we fixed the whole admin-role story.
- Marcus: if we touch the role label itself, that needs proof before anyone writes it up.
- Morgan: keep current Mercury release language disciplined; no broad claims from a string change.

Status at end of call

- Role-label standardization question: unresolved.
- Release language condition: staging proof first if anything from this review is mentioned at all.

Mercury activation-copy review — prep note
Tuesday, August 5, 2025

Purpose

Review the final evidence packet and agree on the next bounded copy test. This is not a final copy decision and does not reopen Mercury’s admin-role or permissions model.

Current evidence

- Nine July onboarding recordings reviewed.
- Five showed hesitation at the same setup-guide/admin sentence.
- In all five, the source-owner cue was visible and the product state was correct.
- Two users proceeded after the facilitator pointed to the cue; three waited for an admin.
- Observed reactions included:
  - “So I need the admin to do this part?”
  - “I’m not the admin, right?”
  - “I’ll wait for our workspace admin.”
- No one asked for granular roles, custom admin policy, or a role editor.

Working read

The evidence supports a copy/activation-clarity issue: the setup-guide sentence may be directing source owners toward an admin even when they can proceed themselves.

Treat that as the hypothesis to test, not as a settled product diagnosis.

Packet

https://docs.mock/doc_1791065065565

Suggested meeting flow

1. Priya walks through the five clips and the exact pause language.
2. Confirm the visible source-owner cue and product state in each example.
3. Separate the user-facing wording problem from any actual implementation or state problem.
4. Compare a small number of possible copy directions, including source-owner-first wording.
5. Agree on what should be tested next and what evidence would change the current read.

Decision prompts

- What wording most clearly tells a source owner that they can proceed, while still giving a non-owner the correct next step?
- What is the smallest follow-up test that would tell us whether the hesitation is reduced without changing the underlying admin model?

Boundaries

- Activation-copy evidence only.
- No admin-model, permissions, or role-scope change.
- Do not infer a product-state defect unless the source-owner cue is missing, misleading, or not actionable in the actual path.
- If Jake is involved, keep his role to a bounded copy/product-state implementation check with the clips attached.
- Keep Leo out unless the review finds a state mismatch or a disappearing cue.
- Do not turn this into a broader settings, role, or onboarding redesign.

Desired meeting output

- A clearly stated copy hypothesis to test.
- The specific state/cue checks required before testing.
- An owner for the follow-up sample.
- A rough sample shape or success signal, without declaring the copy treatment final.

1) Purpose
This packet is intended to give Evergreen Bank a concise procurement/security review summary for the current Mercury design-partner deployment: commercial model, present login/setup scope, current admin/security posture for the bounded launch experience, and known enterprise-readiness gaps that remain outside launch scope.

2) Commercial model
Mercury is currently priced on monthly active developer usage, not purchased seats and not directory size.

Current bands:
- Pilot: $2,500/month platform minimum, including up to 50 monthly active developers
- Growth: $7,500/month platform minimum, including up to 200 monthly active developers
- Overage: $1,000 per additional 50 monthly active developers

Counting notes:
- monthly active developer usage is the pricing driver
- Scaffold internal/test users do not count toward usage

3) Current Mercury scope
Current Mercury design-partner scope is the live bounded experience now in use:

- setup flow oriented around connecting a real source
- preview/sample data available only as preview behavior and not activating by itself
- first live sync path in product

- first_live_sync_completed within 7 days

What is not in current launch scope:
- SSO
- deeper admin controls beyond the current bounded experience
- audit history for admin changes
- expanded enterprise/security packaging beyond the current design-partner flow

4) Current login / setup experience
For the present Mercury flow, user access is handled through magic links and org invites. Session handling is Clerk-backed. The intended path is:
1. invited user enters through magic link / invite flow
2. user lands in the Mercury workspace context
3. user connects a real source
4. user reaches first live sync

Preview/sample behavior may be shown during evaluation, but preview/sample-only behavior does not activate the account and should not be described as equivalent to real source connection or live sync completion.

5) Current admin / security readiness for present scope
Current readiness should be described as sufficient for the bounded design-partner experience, not as a full enterprise admin/security package.

- access is handled through the current magic-link and invite flow
- org-level invitation exists in the current Mercury experience
- the launch experience is bounded and intentionally narrower than a full enterprise rollout
- current product facts should be reviewed against the present scope, not against a broader enterprise-control checklist

What we should not imply in this draft:
- that Mercury already includes full enterprise-ready login controls
- that current admin behavior covers all enterprise audit/control requirements
- that later-scope items are part of the live launch package today

- SSO timing
- audit history for admin changes
- clearer separation between admin permissions and billing-owner controls
- procurement material that can stand on its own without Morgan or Devon live-explaining it

input.title: Late-deploy coverage note: what Q3 2022 should have taught us
input.body:
The Q3 2022 weekend incident was not random bad luck. Its blast radius was small and recovery happened at a favorable time, but the underlying failure was the same one we saw again in March: a late deploy without guaranteed coverage and a clear rollback path.

The lesson we should have written down then was simple: a lucky recovery does not make the deployment process safe. No late deploy without explicit coverage and a fast, known rollback path. If coverage cannot be guaranteed, the deploy waits. For an unavoidable late-Friday deploy, the whole team stays on standby.

March turned the same gap into an 18-hour incident. The problem was not primarily the size of the change; it was the timing, unclear ownership, and fuzzy rollback path.

results.content:
Marcus’s auth-rewrite rollout checklist is here:

Auth rewrite rollout checklist
Owner: Marcus
Date: 2023-10-11
Scope: API v2 auth path only. Existing API behavior remains GraphQL + JWT on the client-facing side; this rollout changes how session revalidation happens behind that path.

Status snapshot
- Staging pass completed on the happy path.
- JWT refresh behavior looks correct in the tested web flows.
- Rollback path is defined, but I have not finished the last prod-like dry run on the rollback toggle.
- Release note wording is still open, mainly on whether we name Clerk directly or keep the note provider-neutral.

Preflight items
[x] Staging login -> dashboard load on API v2 with fresh JWT
[x] Expired JWT on API v2 GraphQL request triggers background revalidation and returns a fresh token without user-visible signout
[x] Retry-once refresh path matches the already-live auth refresh retry behavior
[x] Accepted-org-invite flow still lands the user in the correct org after session revalidation
[x] Existing browser session survives page refresh after token expiry
[ ] Canary owner + 30-minute watch window confirmed
[ ] Rollback toggle exercised end-to-end in prod-like config
[ ] Final release note wording approved for #eng-releases

Clerk session revalidation steps
1. Start with an existing signed-in web session on API v2.
2. Let the short-lived JWT age past TTL or force-expire it in the browser.
3. Hit a normal GraphQL read and then a write.
4. Expected result: request chain gets a fresh JWT through the session revalidation path; user stays signed in; org context does not change.
5. Confirm session revalidation does not bounce the user to auth, lose the selected workspace, or break invite-derived org membership.
6. Watch for a one-request 401 blip versus a sticky 401 loop; only the sticky case is a rollout stopper.

JWT refresh checks
- Fresh-token path: no regression in normal API v2 reads/writes.
- Expired-token path: refresh occurs once, request succeeds, no manual retry needed.
- Concurrent-tab check: second tab should accept the new token without drifting into repeated 401s.
- Metrics to watch during canary: 401 rate, refresh retry count, session revalidation latency, and any spike in auth-related support pings.

Rollback flag
- Rollback is a single toggle that disables Clerk-backed session revalidation and returns API v2 to the legacy validator path.
- Intended use: only if canary shows sustained auth failures, sticky 401 loops, or org-context mismatches.
- Expected rollback behavior: JWT format exposed to API v2 callers stays the same; the internal session source changes back.
- Still open: I want one more dry run to confirm the toggle clears cleanly without leaving mixed auth state on already-warm pods.

Draft release-note wording
Option A — provider named
API v2 auth now uses Clerk-backed session revalidation behind the scenes for expired sessions. No customer action is expected.

Option B — provider-neutral
API v2 auth now revalidates expired sessions more consistently in the background. No customer action is expected.

Open wording note
I’m not sure whether naming Clerk in the release note is useful precision for the team or unnecessary provider callout. Everything else in the note can stay narrow to API v2 auth behavior.

Please review it and DM Marcus the remaining go/no-go questions in our internal team chat. Also prepare a narrow #eng-releases note that describes the API v2 auth behavior change without making Clerk customer-facing positioning or implying any customer action is needed.

# Atlas/API v2 support-contract examples — draft 2026-07-30

## 1. Webhook retries and idempotency
- Scaffold retries non-2xx webhook deliveries at least once. Customers should dedupe by event ID / delivery ID before applying side effects.
- Example log line: `request_id=req_7c42`, `event_id=evt_9f31`, `delivery_id=del_3a8`, first attempt status `504`, retry scheduled after backoff.
- Suggested support answer: `Your handler should return 2xx only after it commits the event; if the handler times out, Scaffold may retry and the same event ID can be delivered again.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `We are evaluating future exactly-once semantics for enterprise connectors.`

## 2. Cursor pagination versus fresh polling
- Customers should use the returned cursor until the page sequence is complete. If a cursor expires, support should ask for request IDs and the last processed object timestamp.
- Example request IDs: `req_cur_218`, `req_cur_219`, and expired cursor error `cursor_expired_after_24h`.
- Suggested support answer: `Resume from your last durable checkpoint rather than running a full fresh poll unless you have lost the checkpoint entirely.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Fresh polling is acceptable until cursor APIs are more mature.`

## 3. JWT clock skew and JWKS cache freshness
- API v2 customer docs say JWT `nbf` values should allow up to five minutes of clock skew and sample timestamps should not be copied into production tokens.
- Example support read: customer server clock was about seven minutes ahead, and JWKS cache was still using the previous signing key after rotation.
- Suggested support answer: `Sync the server clock, refresh JWKS cache, and send request IDs only if failures continue after those checks.`
- Draft line that worries Morgan: `Support can allow wider clock windows during enterprise migrations if setup is blocked.`

2. Kibo care in Oakland
   - Confirm a primary sitter for the full travel window and a backup who can access the apartment.
   - Do a meet-and-greet/run-through: food, walks, medication if any, apartment details, keys, alarm, and emergency contacts.
   - Put this in the written care note: “Kibo cannot have poultry-based food or treats. No chicken, turkey, duck, poultry meal, or similar ingredient. If the label is unclear, do not feed it—ask Morgan.”

Date: April 28, 2023

What worked:
The all-hands shifted from the original IMP-C Q&A into a demo-day-style team show-and-tell. Each team received 5 minutes.

Comparison with the Q&A attempt:
The IMP-C Q&A fell flat: the room was silent for the first 30 minutes. The group abandoned that format halfway through and switched to the team show-and-tells, which got people talking and re-engaged the room.

Takeaway:
Short, time-boxed team show-and-tells were more effective for participation than the open Q&A format used that day.
