results.content:
Sofia —

Using only the existing September/October Mercury cohort package:

1. Cohort scope

The September and October cohorts include accounts that entered the defined, bounded Mercury product flow represented in the package. This is not a broader pipeline view and does not include prospective accounts outside that flow.

2. Activation definition

For an outside reader, “activated within 7 days” means that, within the first seven days, the account either connected a real source or completed its first live sync. Each account is counted once.

The activation numerator excludes sample imports, preview-only behavior, invites sent or accepted, preview views, source selection without connection, and similar first-week motion that does not reach a real source connection or first live sync.

3. October: 19/27 versus 16/27

The October cohort had 19 of 27 accounts activated within seven days and 16 of 27 completing a first live sync within seven days. The full three-account difference is accounts that connected a real source within seven days but had not completed their first live sync during that same window.

There is no additional transitional state that should be read as activation. Preview/sample activity, invite-only activity, and source-selected-but-not-connected activity remain outside the count.

4. Week-one focus and expansion caveat

The package stays week-one focused because it is intended to show the initial real-source and first-live-sync path. Late-October accounts do not yet support a clean longer-window expansion read on the same basis.

The direct read is that activation and the initial administrator path improved, while expansion beyond that initial setup remains uneven. The cohort results should not be read as showing that broader team usage or downstream expansion is solved.

5. External versus internal views

Weekly cuts and sample-preview diagnostics remain internal operating views. They are not part of the board or investor view, and we are not sending them as part of this diligence follow-up.

Best,
Anna

input.title: October 2023 Mercury Cohort: Seven-Day Activation Methodology
input.body:
Purpose

This document explains the October 2023 Mercury cohort’s week-one activation and first-live-sync counts using the existing bounded-flow methodology.

Cohort and window

- Cohort: 27 accounts that entered the bounded Mercury flow.
- Measurement window: the first seven days after each account entered that flow.
- Each account is counted once.

Definitions

- Activated within seven days: the account either connected a real source or completed its first live sync within the seven-day window.
- First live sync within seven days: the account completed its first live sync within that same window.
- Sample imports, preview-only behavior, invites sent or accepted, preview views, source selection without connection, and similar activity do not count as activation.

Results

- Seven-day activation: 19 of 27 accounts (70%).
- Seven-day first live sync: 16 of 27 accounts (59%).
- Difference: 3 accounts (3 of 27).

Why the counts differ

The activation measure is broader than the first-live-sync measure: it counts either a real-source connection or a completed first live sync. The 16 accounts that completed first live sync are therefore included in the 19 activated accounts. The remaining 3 accounts connected a real source within seven days but had not completed their first live sync during that same window.

Thus, 19/27 is not an unexplained leakage figure or a preview- or invite-only bucket; it is the union of qualifying real-source connection and first-live-sync events. The result is week-one focused and should not be read as evidence that downstream expansion or broader team usage is solved.

input.title: Archive Note — March 15, 2023 Production Outage
input.body:
March 15, 2023 Production Outage

Archive date: September 14, 2026

Mechanism

- A small, roughly ten-line change introduced a new request path behind an edge flag.
- When a request entered the new path and encountered a cache miss, it fell through to the old entitlement check.
- The request then retried against the worker pool. Retries accumulated there, creating queue buildup and contributing to API 500s and stuck customer jobs.
- Each affected request fanned out into roughly 6–8 internal calls, so the operational load was much larger than the diff suggested.

Why impact was uneven across tenants

- The bad branch was conditional: only some tenants reached it. Tenants whose requests did not take that branch were largely unaffected, while tenants that did reach it experienced the retry and fan-out behavior.
- Because affected requests generated multiple internal calls, a relatively limited set of tenant requests could create disproportionate worker-pool and queue pressure.
- The mixed tenant population made aggregate dashboards look partially normal for too long, delaying a clear read of the blast radius.
- The available incident record does not preserve the precise tenant-selection predicate for the bad branch; it does establish that branch reachability, rather than a uniform global failure, explains the uneven tenant impact.

Response and recovery context

- Devon investigated traces, and Priya rolled traffic back using the edge flag.
- Stragglers remained because jobs had already been queued.
- The outage lasted about 18 hours end-to-end, with full recovery by midday March 16.

Archival lesson

Do not ship branchy authentication or entitlement logic behind a flag without replaying it against prod-like traffic first. A small diff can have a large, asymmetric blast radius when one request expands into many internal calls.

Folder: archive

checks.observed:
March 15, 2023 Production Outage

Archive date: September 14, 2026

Mechanism

- A small, roughly ten-line change introduced a new request path behind an edge flag.
- When a request entered the new path and encountered a cache miss, it fell through to the old entitlement check.
- The request then retried against the worker pool. Retries accumulated there, creating queue buildup and contributing to API 500s and stuck customer jobs.
- Each affected request fanned out into roughly 6–8 internal calls, so the operational load was much larger than the diff suggested.

Why impact was uneven across tenants

- The bad branch was conditional: only some tenants reached it. Tenants whose requests did not take that branch were largely unaffected, while tenants that did reach it experienced the retry and fan-out behavior.
- Because affected requests generated multiple internal calls, a relatively limited set of tenant requests could create disproportionate worker-pool and queue pressure.
- The mixed tenant population made aggregate dashboards look partially normal for too long, delaying a clear read of the blast radius.
- The available incident record does not preserve the precise tenant-selection predicate for the bad branch; it does establish that branch reachability, rather than a uniform global failure, explains the uneven tenant impact.

Response and recovery context

- Devon investigated traces, and Priya rolled traffic back using the edge flag.
- Stragglers remained because jobs had already been queued.
- The outage lasted about 18 hours end-to-end, with full recovery by midday March 16.

Archival lesson

Do not ship branchy authentication or entitlement logic behind a flag without replaying it against prod-like traffic first. A small diff can have a large, asymmetric blast radius when one request expands into many internal calls.
checks.reason: The note states that the new request path encountered a cache miss, fell through to the old entitlement check, and retried against the worker pool where retries accumulated. It also says only some tenants reached the bad branch and each affected request fanned out into roughly 6–8 internal calls.

excerpts:
Tuesday working session: Compass v0.1 signal definitions

Participants: Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo, Sarah  
Goal: Turn each signal into a bounded operating rule, not a dashboard, hiring trigger, or roadmap expansion.

1. Frame and guardrails — 5 min

- Compass v0.1 is an internal decision aid built from current evidence.
- Keep the read directional and source-linked.
- No board dashboard or new board reporting surface.
- No new hiring lane, requisition, or team-shape decision from a single account or signal.
- One repeated pattern per row; separate product, support, procurement, and source-quality evidence.

2. Signal review — 15 min each

Signal A: Evergreen paid-pilot adoption

Answer:
- What action should this trigger, if any?
- Who sees it: product owner, account owner, support, leadership?
- What evidence travels with it, and what caveat prevents over-reading?
- What must be true in the Evergreen account note and source packet?
- What are we explicitly not building: custom roadmap work, enterprise-readiness promise, or hiring response?

Signal B: Renewal and expansion evidence

Answer:
- What behavior qualifies as genuine renewal or expansion evidence?
- What action should this trigger, and at what threshold or repeat count?
- Who sees it, and who owns follow-up?
- What evidence and caveat travel with it, including timing, cohort, and one-off-account limits?
- What account note/source quality is required to distinguish repeatable expansion from anecdote?
- What are we explicitly not building: a sales forecast from weak evidence, a broad GTM motion, or bespoke customer commitments?

Signal C: Nadia’s account-source quality

Answer:
- What action should a clean, repeatable source pattern trigger?
- Who sees the result: Nadia, Sarah, Devon, product, or leadership?
- What evidence and caveat travel with it?
- What must the account note contain: earliest attributable source, source date, original thread/evidence link, and reason for any correction?
- What happens when the source is unknown or unrecoverable?
- What are we explicitly not building: channel-performance claims, a new CRM taxonomy, or a hiring lane based on one cleaned snapshot?

3. Cross-signal routing check — 10 min

For every approved row, confirm:

- Signal owner
- Account-note owner
- Evidence source and link
- Caveat
- Audience
- Triggered action, if any
- “No action yet” condition
- Explicit non-outcome

Default routing:

- Anna: metric, cohort, and retention caveats
- Nadia: synthesis and weekly internal read
- Sarah: live-account continuity and account-note hygiene
- Jake: product sequencing and current-product truth
- Leo: platform/release evidence and system-behavior verification

4. Close — 5 min

Leave with:

- A small set of approved Compass rows
- One bounded action or no-action rule per signal
- Named evidence and source-quality requirements
- A parking lot for unresolved product, packaging, or customer-specific questions

Final boundary: Compass v0.1 remains an internal, source-linked operating read.

# Compass v0.1 — first working-session agenda

Date: January 21, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

## Purpose

Move Compass v0.1 from abstract “useful signals” to a small set of bounded operating rules: when a signal appears, what should happen, who should see it, and what evidence is sufficient. Keep the read internal, directional, source-linked, and narrow enough to ship or test.

## Opening frame and guardrails — 5 minutes

- Compass v0.1 is an internal decision aid built from current evidence, not a declaration of broad product or market truth.
- Definitions, caveats, confidence, and provenance stay attached to every signal.
- Separate product weakness, support evidence, procurement drag, admin confusion, observed usage, and internal inference; do not flatten them into one score or label.
- A signal matters only if it leads to a named owner and a concrete account-team, customer-growth, support, or product action—or to an explicit “no action yet” decision.
- Check the data/platform seam before anything is shown outside the current team.

## Signal review — 15 minutes each

### 1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction evidence

Working shape:

- Identify the specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion behind apparent renewal risk.
- Point to a named account-owner follow-up rather than merely labeling an account “at risk.”
- Keep true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag distinct.

Questions to answer:

- What action should this trigger for the real account, and who is the named owner?
- Who sees it first: account owner, support, product, Nadia, or another internal audience?
- What evidence travels with the signal, and what caveat prevents “renewal risk” from being over-read?
- What must be true in the account note or source packet before this becomes an account-team script rather than an internal FYI?
- Can the record distinguish a customer statement, support readout, observed account behavior, and internal interpretation?
- What is the minimum evidence package required before Nadia approves follow-up?
- What condition means “no action yet”?
- What are we explicitly not building: a binary risk label, a generalized risk score, a broad procurement or product diagnosis, or a customer-specific roadmap commitment?

### 2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt

Working shape:

- Focus on the post-first-live-sync moment and the next useful action after first real traction.
- Trigger only after the first live sync is actually live.
- Make teammate-invite and admin-role basics visible enough for the follow-up to be grounded in actual account state.
- Distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage.

Questions to answer:

- What behavior qualifies as a real post-first-live-sync expansion opportunity?
- What is the smallest useful prompt or account-team/customer-growth script that should follow?
- At what exact point may the trigger fire, and what evidence prevents it from firing too early?
- Who sees it and who owns the next step?
- What evidence and caveat travel with it, including the difference between observed usage and inferred readiness?
- Has Leo verified that the underlying event path and data/platform seam are reliable enough for the current audience?
- What condition means “no action yet”?
- What are we explicitly not building: another metrics view, generic upsell language, a broad growth workflow, a new product surface, or a bespoke customer commitment?

### 3. Account-note source quality for customer-growth follow-up

Working shape:

- Treat source hygiene as a gating input, not cleanup after the fact.
- Classify the underlying note as reliable, mixed, or too thin before using a signal.
- Preserve provenance: customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation.
- If note quality is weak, make the caveat explicit or keep the signal internal.

Questions to answer:

- What action should a clean, repeatable source pattern trigger, if any?
- Who sees the result: Nadia, Sarah, the account owner, product, or leadership?
- What evidence and caveat travel with the signal?
- What must the account note contain before it can feed real follow-up: attributable source, date/recency, original thread or evidence link, and any correction reason?
- How will Sarah distinguish a reliable, traceable note from a mixed or too-thin note?
- Can the record separate customer fact from support fact, observed usage, and internal inference?
- What happens when the source is unknown, unrecoverable, or contradicted?
- What condition means “no action yet”?
- What are we explicitly not building: channel-performance claims, a new CRM taxonomy, a clean-looking metrics layer that hides weak evidence, or a hiring decision based on one cleaned snapshot?

## Cross-signal routing check — 10 minutes

For every approved signal row, confirm:

- Signal definition and owner
- Triggered action or explicit “no action yet” condition
- First audience and follow-up owner
- Account-note owner
- Evidence source and link
- Caveat and confidence/provenance label
- Data/platform seam check, where applicable
- Explicit non-outcome or non-build

Default ownership:

- Anna: signal definitions, metric/cohort/retention caveats
- Nadia: synthesis, customer-growth/account-team follow-up logic, weekly internal read
- Sarah: live-account continuity, account-note hygiene, source classification
- Jake: product sequencing and current-product truth; prevent scope expansion
- Leo: platform/release evidence and system-behavior verification

## Close — 5 minutes

Leave with:

- A small set of approved Compass v0.1 rows
- One bounded action or no-action rule per signal
- Named evidence and source-quality requirements
- Open product, packaging, or customer-specific questions parked for later
- A clear escalation to Morgan if the work starts looking like a dashboard or platform build

## Explicit limits on what we were building

- No board dashboard and no new board-reporting surface.
- No new hiring lane, requisition, or team-shape decision from a single account or signal.
- No prettier internal dashboard or metrics-surface polish pass as the goal.
- No broad roadmap expansion, custom roadmap work, enterprise-readiness promise, or bespoke customer commitment from a signal.
- No generic upsell motion, broad GTM system, sales forecast from weak evidence, or customer-facing claim of repeatability.
- No flattening of distinct evidence types into one score or binary risk label.
- No platform build: only the minimum seam work needed to test the renewal/admin-friction evidence and post-sync expansion prompt.

Final boundary: Compass v0.1 is an internal, source-linked operating read about signal interpretation and follow-up behavior—not a board dashboard, roadmap commitment, hiring trigger, or broad product/platform build.

- What condition means “no action yet”?
- What are we explicitly not building: another metrics view, generic upsell language, a broad growth workflow, a new product surface, or a bespoke customer commitment?

### 3. Account-note source quality for customer-growth follow-up

Working shape:

- Treat source hygiene as a gating input, not cleanup after the fact.
- Classify the underlying note as reliable, mixed, or too thin before using a signal.
- Preserve provenance: customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation.
- If note quality is weak, make the caveat explicit or keep the signal internal.

Questions to answer:

- What action should a clean, repeatable source pattern trigger, if any?
- Who sees the result: Nadia, Sarah, the account owner, product, or leadership?
- What evidence and caveat travel with the signal?
- What must the account note contain before it can feed real follow-up: attributable source, date/recency, original thread or evidence link, and any correction reason?
- How will Sarah distinguish a reliable, traceable note from a mixed or too-thin note?
- Can the record separate customer fact from support fact, observed usage, and internal inference?
- What happens when the source is unknown, unrecoverable, or contradicted?
- What condition means “no action yet”?
- What are we explicitly not building: channel-performance claims, a new CRM taxonomy, a clean-looking metrics layer that hides weak evidence, or a hiring decision based on one cleaned snapshot?

## Cross-signal routing check — 10 minutes

For every approved signal row, confirm:

- Signal definition and owner
- Triggered action or explicit “no action yet” condition
- First audience and follow-up owner
- Account-note owner
- Evidence source and link
- Caveat and confidence/provenance label
- Data/platform seam check, where applicable
- Explicit non-outcome or non-build

Default ownership:

- Anna: signal definitions, metric/cohort/retention caveats
- Nadia: synthesis, customer-growth/account-team follow-up logic, weekly internal read
- Sarah: live-account continuity, account-note hygiene, source classification
- Jake: product sequencing and current-product truth; prevent scope expansion
- Leo: platform/release evidence and system-behavior verification

## Close — 5 minutes

Leave with:

- A small set of approved Compass v0.1 rows
- One bounded action or no-action rule per signal
- Named evidence and source-quality requirements
- Open product, packaging, or customer-specific questions parked for later
- A clear escalation to Morgan if the work starts looking like a dashboard or platform build

## Explicit limits on what we were building

- No board dashboard and no new board-reporting surface.
- No new hiring lane, requisition, or team-shape decision from a single account or signal.
- No prettier internal dashboard or metrics-surface polish pass as the goal.
- No broad roadmap expansion, custom roadmap work, enterprise-readiness promise, or bespoke customer commitment from a signal.
- No generic upsell motion, broad GTM system, sales forecast from weak evidence, or customer-facing claim of repeatability.
- No flattening of distinct evidence types into one score or binary risk label.
- No platform build: only the minimum seam work needed to test the renewal/admin-friction evidence and post-sync expansion prompt.

Final boundary: Compass v0.1 is an internal, source-linked operating read about signal interpretation and follow-up behavior—not a board dashboard, roadmap commitment, hiring trigger, or broad product/platform build.

input.title: Archive note — 2024 customer-growth / GTM leader search
input.body:
Date of archive note: 2026-09-14

Historical scope

In February–March 2024, the customer-growth / GTM leader search was the first new leadership-search lane scoped after the operating reset. It was chosen instead of immediately reopening the second Mercury engineering requisition. The search was intended to add a hands-on builder who could turn Mercury and Evergreen-like design-partner and enterprise-adoption learning into a repeatable, measurable customer-growth motion.

What the search was meant to achieve

- Identify the customer profiles and use cases where the product created repeatable value.
- Convert onboarding, activation, first live use, broader-team adoption, expansion, and renewal learning into a practical operating playbook.
- Run bounded evaluations using the product and commercial structure Scaffold could support at the time, with explicit success criteria and decision points.
- Separate generalizable product, security, procurement, packaging, and onboarding gaps from one-off customer requests or services work.
- Create disciplined feedback loops among customer conversations, product, engineering, commercial work, and growth metrics.
- Establish an evidence-led cadence for customer health, usage, qualified pipeline, adoption, expansion, and retention.
- Recommend an initial ICP, qualification rules, adoption milestones, expansion signals, and a measured six- and twelve-month path before adding broader capacity.
- Reduce founder dependence and improve repeatability without overstating retention, expansion, enterprise readiness, or the strength of the evidence.

The role was therefore a customer-growth and operating-discipline build around observed customer evidence—not a generic sales-leadership search. The eventual approved remit, after the process was completed, remained bounded around repeatable Mercury and Evergreen-style learning and evidence from the product available at the time.

What the search did not authorize

- It was not a generic VP Sales mandate, a field-sales build, or permission to stand up a conventional sales organization immediately.
- It did not authorize bespoke product promises, roadmap commitments, custom implementations, or dates made to close an individual account.
- It did not authorize customer-specific pricing or packaging carveouts, procurement concessions, or other exceptions outside approved company policy.
- It did not authorize turning customer accounts into ongoing roadmap negotiations or making one-off commitments the operating system.
- It did not reopen product strategy, expand product scope, or treat customer requests as commitments; requests were inputs to a learning and prioritization process.
- It did not authorize a sales-kickoff claim, an enterprise-proof claim, a customer-facing launch, or a claim that repeatability had already been established.
- It did not authorize broader hiring—such as AE, CSM, RevOps, demand-generation, or additional engineering capacity—without a separate evidence-based operating decision.
- Candidates in process were not to be described as a hiring outcome until fit and references were complete; the search itself was not proof that the model had been validated.

Archive interpretation

The durable decision was to test whether Mercury / Evergreen-style pull could become a repeatable adoption, expansion, and renewal motion while preserving product-truth boundaries. The search authorized learning, bounded execution, evidence synthesis, and recommendations. It did not authorize promises, exceptions, a broader commercial build, or stronger growth claims than the customer evidence supported.

input.title: Historical Honeycomb Alert Handling Note — December 23, 2023–January 1, 2024
input.body:
Historical Honeycomb alert handling
Coverage window: Saturday, December 23, 2023 through Monday, January 1, 2024
Normal scheduling resumed Tuesday, January 2, 2024.

Purpose
This note records the holiday-period handling for Honeycomb alerts: preserve the existing monitoring posture, keep the on-call path clear, reserve founder escalation for material cases, and summarize a quiet week rather than generating unnecessary noise.

Thresholds
- Keep the existing Honeycomb alert thresholds unchanged throughout the coverage window.
- Do not lower, raise, mute, or otherwise retune thresholds merely because of the holiday schedule.
- Non-urgent alert cleanup or threshold work can wait until January.

Paging
- Page the named engineering on-call owner first: Marcus.
- Use the documented backup path if needed: Leo Park.
- Handle active production issues through the named owner and backup path rather than paging founders directly.

Escalation
- Escalate to Morgan only when there is confirmed customer impact, or when the on-call path cannot reach anyone after the documented owner/backup path has been tried.
- A slow acknowledgment alone is not a reason to bypass the path; continue using the named owner and backup process.
- Non-production flaps and other alert noise without confirmed customer impact remain in the normal on-call process and do not require founder escalation.

Quiet-week reporting
- If the week remains quiet, roll the week’s alerts into Monday’s digest instead of sending separate holiday-period noise reports.
- The digest should distinguish alert flaps from confirmed customer impact and note any meaningful acknowledgment or escalation issue.
- Example historical reduced-week reporting: two non-production alert flaps, no confirmed customer impact, and one slow acknowledgment were reported; the handling direction remained unchanged—keep current thresholds, page the named on-call owner first, escalate only for confirmed customer impact or an unreachable owner, and put other noise in the Monday digest.

Source note
This is a retrospective operating note based on the holiday coverage guidance issued December 21, 2023 and the reduced-week Honeycomb digest/escalation follow-up from December 26, 2023.

The all-hands ran long and these are my raw notes.

Q1 all-hands — Morgan raw notes
Date: 2024-04-03

Opening
- “Q1 was about making Mercury real enough to learn from, not declaring victory.”
- Keep the post-raise line tight: more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story.
- Need to answer scope questions directly, not with general optimism.

Mercury update
- Current release focus: admin controls, live-sync reliability, invited-member handoffs, and evidence quality before Q3 launch planning.
- Weekly Mercury truth check stays on support edges, live-sync trust, admin friction, and what is materially changing in product.
- Enterprise-readiness review stays a separate lane from current Mercury release work; do not contaminate release notes with broader enterprise scope.
- Leo’s current platform/seams read: live-sync trust looks stable; overnight warning spikes are watch items unless we reproduce an actual state bug.
- Recovered-state wording only if the copy diff stays tiny and isolated.
- Invited-member handoff confusion stays with Priya and Jake unless it becomes a real state/platform bug.
- Owner reminder if asked: Jake = Mercury execution and launch evidence; Leo = platform seams and release discipline; Priya = activation/onboarding UX; Anna = retention evidence; Devon with Sarah = enterprise-readiness commercial packaging; Morgan = board narrative and hiring sequence.

Devon retention slide
- Week-four retained activity is improving for the current Mercury cohort.
- Sample is still small.
- Package read is not a settled enterprise-expansion story.
- Important to say “improving” without turning it into “proven.”

Customer-growth hiring mention
- Nadia has accepted Head of Customer Growth and starts Apr 15.
- Do not pull her into customer-facing work before then.
- First-90-day frame: build a repeatable customer-growth motion around Mercury activation, Evergreen-style enterprise-readiness signals, expansion failure modes, and handoffs with Sarah Kim and Devon.
- This is not a signal that product strategy changes immediately.

Employee questions captured verbatim
Q1. “Are we narrowing Mercury scope, or adding enterprise admin work on top of the existing Q3 launch?”
Q2. “Who owns support load when Evergreen finds workflow confusion during testing?”
Q3. “Are we still treating live-sync as green if there are overnight warning spikes?”
Q4. “Does Nadia starting mean product strategy changes immediately?”
Q5. “How do we keep release evidence from becoming another parallel process every team has to feed?”

Answer notes / talk track
- Q1: narrowing current Mercury scope. Bounded admin-control work in the release plan stays in; broader enterprise-readiness work stays separate.
- Q2: Priya owns workflow/onboarding confusion, Jake owns Mercury execution and support triage, Leo only if it reproduces as an actual state bug.
- Q3: green watch item is still green only because current live-sync trust looks stable; warning spikes alone do not change the read without reproduced customer-state impact.
- Q4: no immediate product-strategy reset when Nadia starts; her role is to build repeatable customer-growth motion, not reopen bespoke enterprise promises.
- Q5: evidence should come from existing release/support work, not a second reporting system every team feeds.

Closing note
- “Answer with scope discipline, not pep talk.”

Please turn them into a tight internal recap that answers the actual employee questions. Keep Nadia to the bounded hiring mention; don’t make it a strategy memo.

input.title: Mercury planning archive — May 2023
input.body:
May 2023 planning archive note

Operating work coordination

Mercury was treated as the operating spine. Day-to-day coordination ran through Jake’s weekly operating list, with one visible list of blockers, owners, and decisions due. The May 9 Mercury weekly was explicitly limited to product and operating work: admin invites, activation instrumentation, and account-level permissions. Jake owned the weekly operating cadence; Priya handled UX confusion and onboarding clarity; Anna marked fresh versus noisy retention data and cleaned up activation definitions; Morgan was pulled in for actual scope calls and unblock decisions. The May 12 offsite and subsequent protected operating-work blocks fed into this same execution lane. Customer Success blocker and admin-pain digests, customer follow-up, and activation-mapping reviews were used as operating inputs rather than investor materials.

Investor-deck prioritization

The investor deck was kept in a separate lane and deliberately deferred while launch inputs were tightened. The priority order was launch work first, deck work second—not as a defensive posture, but because Mercury’s proof points, instrumentation, and retention/activation framing needed to be cleaner before reopening the broader investor narrative. The corrected activation logic and weekly operating cuts were for internal operating use only; they were not to be back-doored into a board note, external chart, or investor story. In practical terms, Mercury’s weekly was not a venue for investor or deck detours, and operating evidence had to stabilize before deck work resumed.

Spent time in the sandbox on the two hosted paths we keep circling for Mercury auth. Not trying to re-open custom auth; this is just the practical readout on where Clerk is clean, where Auth0 is cleaner, and what still feels unresolved before we talk live.

- Sessions
  - Clerk: fastest path to a working session flow. I had middleware + server check working quickly, and the happy path feels boring in a good way.
  - Auth0: also works, but it took more setup to get to the same place. More knobs if we end up needing unusual policy or tenant-specific behavior.
  - Still unproven: session refresh after invite accept or org change.

- Magic links
  - Clerk: easiest end-to-end flow so far. New user + return user behavior was straightforward in the sandbox.
  - Auth0 passwordless: workable, but redirect/state handling was fussier and I hit more did-we-just-lose-the-return-path moments.
  - Need one more pass on link reuse and expiry behavior so support is not guessing on day one.

- Organization invites
  - Clerk's org model maps pretty well to the basic team-invite flow we want.
  - Main edge case: invited person already has a personal workspace, then accepts into a team workspace. That handoff is not fully burned down.
  - Auth0 can do it, but we would own more of the invite and membership stitching ourselves.

- SSO / admin gaps
  - This is still the squishiest area.
  - If Mercury launch only needs normal session auth + invites, Clerk remains the simpler path.
  - If we need deeper admin controls, domain or IdP management, or more enterprise-ish SSO behavior earlier than planned, Auth0 still looks stronger there.

- Pricing caveats
  - Clerk is better on speed right now.
  - I still do not have a satisfying pricing view if usage ramps fast and we end up with a large MAU footprint on top of org features.
  - Auth0 is less pleasant on implementation time, but the enterprise/contract shape may be less surprising later.

Discord — #eng-team
2023-06-07 08:14 PT
Rishi Patel

Mercury auth v0.2 readout prep

Spent time in the sandbox on the two hosted paths we keep circling for Mercury auth. Not trying to re-open custom auth; this is just the practical readout on where Clerk is clean, where Auth0 is cleaner, and what still feels unresolved before we talk live.

- Sessions
  - Clerk: fastest path to a working session flow. I had middleware + server check working quickly, and the happy path feels boring in a good way.
  - Auth0: also works, but it took more setup to get to the same place. More knobs if we end up needing unusual policy or tenant-specific behavior.
  - Still unproven: session refresh after invite accept or org change.

- Magic links
  - Clerk: easiest end-to-end flow so far. New user + return user behavior was straightforward in the sandbox.
  - Auth0 passwordless: workable, but redirect/state handling was fussier and I hit more did-we-just-lose-the-return-path moments.
  - Need one more pass on link reuse and expiry behavior so support is not guessing on day one.

- Organization invites
  - Clerk's org model maps pretty well to the basic team-invite flow we want.
  - Main edge case: invited person already has a personal workspace, then accepts into a team workspace. That handoff is not fully burned down.
  - Auth0 can do it, but we would own more of the invite and membership stitching ourselves.

- SSO / admin gaps
  - This is still the squishiest area.
  - If Mercury launch only needs normal session auth + invites, Clerk remains the simpler path.
  - If we need deeper admin controls, domain or IdP management, or more enterprise-ish SSO behavior earlier than planned, Auth0 still looks stronger there.

- Pricing caveats
  - Clerk is better on speed right now.
  - I still do not have a satisfying pricing view if usage ramps fast and we end up with a large MAU footprint on top of org features.
  - Auth0 is less pleasant on implementation time, but the enterprise/contract shape may be less surprising later.

- Staging / deploy note
  - If anyone wants to validate either path on staging, please use the standard pipeline.
  - No one-off shortcut for staging auth testing. I do not want to learn the wrong lesson from a path we would not actually ship.

Happy to turn this into a short walkthrough once people have skimmed.

Hiring debrief: Nadia Singh, Head of Customer Growth

Recommendation

Recommend Nadia Singh for the Head of Customer Growth role.

Nadia is the stronger match for the customer-growth profile we actually settled on: a hands-on builder who can turn Mercury and Evergreen-like learning into a repeatable adoption, expansion, and renewal motion without converting customer requests into bespoke product commitments.

This is not a generic VP Sales hire. The role is to build the system around customer evidence, not to impose a conventional enterprise-sales machine on an early, still-forming product motion.

Comparison against the agreed profile

| Dimension | Nadia Singh | Alternate finalist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Turns design-partner learning into a repeatable motion | Starts with activation evidence, account failure points, handoffs, and durable patterns | Moves quickly toward pipeline, coverage, deal stages, and executive sponsor maps |
| Customer-growth judgment | Separates activation, adoption, expansion, procurement, and product signals | Treats stalled growth primarily as a sales-process or executive-alignment problem |
| Product and promise discipline | Makes current truth, workarounds, owners, and evidence thresholds explicit | More willing to preserve flexibility through concessions or roadmap-adjacent language |
| Stage fit | Comfortable building from incomplete instrumentation and founder-led context | Wants more sales infrastructure, quota mechanics, hiring, and commercial authority sooner |
| Cross-functional boundaries | Keeps Sarah, Devon, Product, and Customer Growth in clear lanes | More likely to collapse boundaries when customer urgency rises |
| Definition of progress | Durable account patterns, broader adoption, and a system that survives beyond founder memory | Pipeline mechanics, account plans, and faster movement toward a conventional revenue model |

Why Nadia is the recommendation

- She began with the evidence needed to understand where customers actually get stuck: activation stages, account-level failure points, owner handoffs, and founder dependencies.
- She proposed one shared operating rhythm across activation friction, adoption, expansion stalls, enterprise-readiness requests, and owner routing rather than separate customer, product, and commercial narratives.
- She consistently distinguished packaging issues, workflow issues, and genuine product gaps. On SSO, admin history, admin-versus-billing ownership, and procurement materials, she stayed within current facts and bounded workarounds.
- Her expansion model was grounded in customer behavior: daily use, broader rollout, admin friction, implementation confidence, procurement drag, and whether value is visible beyond the initial champion.
- She showed the right instinct on incomplete instrumentation: start with account notes and a small set of shared flags, then harden dashboards once the classifications are stable.
- She did not assume Customer Growth should own every customer-adjacent problem. Her handoff model preserves Sarah’s customer continuity, Devon’s commercial and procurement role, and Product’s ownership of product decisions.

Assessment of the alternate finalist

The alternate finalist is capable, but he is optimized for a different company stage and brief.

He reads as a first VP Sales or broader revenue leader who would likely be effective once Scaffold has a clearer sales structure, established deal stages, more formal coverage, and a larger customer-facing team. In this process, though, he repeatedly tried to move from messy customer evidence to pipeline mechanics before establishing where activation and adoption were breaking.

His default responses also leaned toward executive air cover, enterprise packaging, selective concessions, and preserving roadmap flexibility to keep strategic prospects engaged. That is precisely the behavior this role must avoid. It risks turning Mercury and Evergreen into sources of bespoke commitments rather than evidence for a repeatable customer-growth system.

Conclusion

Nadia is the clear recommendation because she understands the actual job:

- Find the customer patterns where the current product creates repeatable value.
- Build a bounded path from evaluation through activation, broader adoption, expansion, and renewal.
- Convert repeated learning into operating discipline.
- Separate generalizable product gaps from one-off requests.
- Protect customer trust by making constraints clear and following through.

Primary watchout

If we move forward, we should make the source inputs and owner boundaries explicit from the start. Nadia should not inherit an undefined founder-cleanup function. Her first 90 days should center on a shared operating rhythm, common language for activation and enterprise-readiness patterns, and a clear system for routing customer evidence to the right owners.

Mercury/Evergreen customer-growth feedback guide

Purpose

Use these categories to turn customer evidence into operating input—not a sales forecast. Every item gets a primary owner route, a named owner, and an optional consult. Customer Growth owns synthesis and pattern quality, not every customer response or fix.

1. Activation friction

What it means:
A workspace stalls before activation or around activation. Activation requires a real source connection or first live sync within seven days.

Typical examples:
- Admin activity occurs, but no source is connected.
- A team is invited, but the workspace never reaches a real value moment.

Route:
- Primary: Priya for activation/setup UX.
- Consult: Jake for Mercury product truth; Anna for cohort or metric caveats.

2. Admin handoff and role confusion

What it means:
Users are unclear about roles, authority, visible admin state, resend/remove actions, or source-workspace wording.

Do not use it for:
A confirmed backend permission bug or a commercial/package dispute.

Route:
- Primary: Support owner for the live response.
- Consult: Priya/Jake for product truth; Sarah for Evergreen account continuity.

3. Procurement/security packaging

What it means:
Current product behavior is being translated into buyer, security, or procurement requirements.

Typical examples:
- Questions about audit wording, SSO timing, admin-versus-billing ownership, or a standalone procurement packet.

Marcus’s auth-rewrite rollout checklist is here:

Auth rewrite rollout checklist
Owner: Marcus
Date: 2023-10-11
Scope: API v2 auth path only. Existing API behavior remains GraphQL + JWT on the client-facing side; this rollout changes how session revalidation happens behind that path.

Status snapshot
- Staging pass completed on the happy path.
- JWT refresh behavior looks correct in the tested web flows.
- Rollback path is defined, but I have not finished the last prod-like dry run on the rollback toggle.
- Release note wording is still open, mainly on whether we name Clerk directly or keep the note provider-neutral.

Preflight items
[x] Staging login -> dashboard load on API v2 with fresh JWT
[x] Expired JWT on API v2 GraphQL request triggers background revalidation and returns a fresh token without user-visible signout
[x] Retry-once refresh path matches the already-live auth refresh retry behavior
[x] Accepted-org-invite flow still lands the user in the correct org after session revalidation
[x] Existing browser session survives page refresh after token expiry
[ ] Canary owner + 30-minute watch window confirmed
[ ] Rollback toggle exercised end-to-end in prod-like config
[ ] Final release note wording approved for #eng-releases

Clerk session revalidation steps
1. Start with an existing signed-in web session on API v2.
2. Let the short-lived JWT age past TTL or force-expire it in the browser.
3. Hit a normal GraphQL read and then a write.
4. Expected result: request chain gets a fresh JWT through the session revalidation path; user stays signed in; org context does not change.
5. Confirm session revalidation does not bounce the user to auth, lose the selected workspace, or break invite-derived org membership.
6. Watch for a one-request 401 blip versus a sticky 401 loop; only the sticky case is a rollout stopper.

JWT refresh checks
- Fresh-token path: no regression in normal API v2 reads/writes.
- Expired-token path: refresh occurs once, request succeeds, no manual retry needed.
- Concurrent-tab check: second tab should accept the new token without drifting into repeated 401s.
- Metrics to watch during canary: 401 rate, refresh retry count, session revalidation latency, and any spike in auth-related support pings.

Rollback flag
- Rollback is a single toggle that disables Clerk-backed session revalidation and returns API v2 to the legacy validator path.
- Intended use: only if canary shows sustained auth failures, sticky 401 loops, or org-context mismatches.
- Expected rollback behavior: JWT format exposed to API v2 callers stays the same; the internal session source changes back.
- Still open: I want one more dry run to confirm the toggle clears cleanly without leaving mixed auth state on already-warm pods.

Draft release-note wording
Option A — provider named
API v2 auth now uses Clerk-backed session revalidation behind the scenes for expired sessions. No customer action is expected.

Option B — provider-neutral
API v2 auth now revalidates expired sessions more consistently in the background. No customer action is expected.

Open wording note
I’m not sure whether naming Clerk in the release note is useful precision for the team or unnecessary provider callout. Everything else in the note can stay narrow to API v2 auth behavior.

Please review it and DM Marcus the remaining go/no-go questions in our internal team chat. Also prepare a narrow #eng-releases note that describes the API v2 auth behavior change without making Clerk customer-facing positioning or implying any customer action is needed.

input.title: March 2023 Board-Framing Case Study — Financing Miss vs. Company Execution
input.body:
March 2023 Board-Framing Case Study

Context
The planned financing round moved later than expected. The board framing needed to explain the timing miss without turning it into either an excuse or an indictment of company execution.

How we separated the issues

- Financing miss: We attributed the timing change to external financing conditions: buyers were freezing, budgets were tightening, and the market had become less willing to underwrite the round on the original schedule. The round’s delay was therefore a timing and market-availability problem, not evidence that the company had failed to deliver the product and team milestones it had committed to.

- Company execution: We assessed execution separately against the operating bar. The team had delivered against the committed product and team work, so we did not describe the financing delay as an execution miss. But we did not use that conclusion to waive operating scrutiny: the March 2 board discussion correctly pressed for sharper retention numbers, because the blended retention story looked cleaner than the underlying evidence. That became a concrete Q2 deliverable, with retention instrumentation and cleanup as a defined workstream.

Board takeaway
The honest message was: the financing slipped because the market and buyer environment changed; execution was broadly on plan; and the company still had real evidence gaps to close. This distinction let the board support management without confusing external timing with operating proof—and without using the financing miss to hide the retention work still required.

excerpts:
Turning enterprise learning into a repeatable motion

“Tell me about an enterprise customer or design partner where the initial deployment worked for one team but had not yet become repeatable across the organization. How did you determine what was genuine product signal versus a one-off champion effect?”

Probes:

- What behavior did you use as the definition of activation?
- What had to happen before you considered the account ready for expansion?
- How did you distinguish usage growth from invitations, demos, or nominal seat growth?
- What did you change in the product, onboarding, qualification, or commercial process?
- How did the learning affect the next account?

Strong signals:

- Uses behavioral milestones rather than vague engagement or logo value.
- Separates bounded evidence from proof of repeatability.
- Can explain a cohort, rollout, or account-learning loop.
- Converts learning into qualification, onboarding, enablement, or expansion changes.

Watch-outs:

- Treats a prominent customer or second department as automatic expansion proof.
- Talks primarily about executive enthusiasm, seats purchased, or logo prestige.
- Cannot explain what changed between the first and subsequent deployments.

2. Adopting a product that is not enterprise-complete

“Imagine a customer can successfully complete the current workflow, but asks for SSO, admin-change audit history, clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation, and a standalone procurement packet before expanding. How would you run that account?”

Probes:

- What would you say the product supports today?
- Which requests would you qualify as launch blockers versus next-phase requirements?
- What would you document for product and engineering?
- What would you refuse to promise?
- How would you decide whether the account is still a fit for the current scope?

Strong signals:

- Anchors the conversation in current product facts.
- Can preserve momentum without disguising product gaps.
- Makes explicit commitments only around actions they control: documentation, discovery, follow-up, or internal review.
- Knows that a roadmap item is not a committed feature or customer-specific exception.
- Is willing to disqualify, pause, or narrow an expansion when the product is not a fit.

Watch-outs:

- Offers dates, bespoke builds, or “we’ll get it on the roadmap” language.
- Treats every security or procurement request as something sales must overcome.
- Says they would “manage expectations” without describing the actual boundary.
- Assumes a large logo justifies special handling.

3. Handling preview interest versus real adoption

“Tell me about a time a customer looked highly engaged during evaluation but failed to reach meaningful production use. How did you identify the difference, and what did you do?”

Probes:

- What was your operational definition of activation?
- Which event or behavior changed your forecast?
- How did you avoid reporting demos, sample data, invitations, or directory size as adoption?
- Did you change onboarding, qualification, pricing, or account ownership afterward?

Strong signals:

- Defines activation through a concrete customer value event.
- Tracks time-to-value and drop-off points.
- Is comfortable reporting weak or ambiguous evidence honestly.
- Builds a feedback loop from failed activation into the next deployment.

4. Creating enterprise adoption without a mature sales org

“You join with no SDR team, limited marketing support, no established sales-ops process, and founders still involved in major accounts. What would you personally build in your first 90 days?”

Probes:

- What would you do yourself before hiring?
- How would you identify the best initial accounts?
- What qualification and disqualification criteria would you establish?
- What would you instrument in the CRM or operating review?
- Which activities would you standardize first?
- What would you deliberately leave unbuilt?

Strong signals:

- Starts with a small number of high-fit accounts and direct customer learning.
- Builds a lightweight operating system: account hypotheses, qualification, stage definitions, activation milestones, expansion criteria, forecast hygiene, and follow-up ownership.
- Can sell, onboard, troubleshoot, and synthesize product feedback personally.
- Understands that hiring should follow evidence of a repeatable motion.
- Avoids importing large-company process before the underlying motion is understood.

Watch-outs:

- First answer is to hire a large team or buy tooling.
- Depends on inbound, brand, marketing-generated pipeline, or founder relationships.
- Cannot describe the minimum viable CRM and review cadence.
- Equates activity volume with a working motion.

5. Founder handoff and cross-functional judgment

“Describe a time you owned an enterprise account alongside a founder or product leader. How did you decide what they should handle, what you owned, and what needed to go back to product or engineering?”

Probes:

- How did you prevent the founder from becoming the permanent account manager?
- How did you protect product and engineering from unqualified customer commitments?
- How did you communicate an uncomfortable product limitation externally?
- What did you put in writing after the meeting?

Strong signals:

- Can use founder access strategically without making it the operating model.
- Keeps customer ownership and follow-up clear.
- Escalates product gaps with evidence, impact, and a recommendation—not pressure or entitlement.
- Documents commitments and non-commitments precisely.

6. Repeatable expansion judgment

“Tell me about an expansion you chose not to pursue—or delayed—even though the account was commercially attractive. What made you say no?”

Probes:

- What evidence was missing?
- Was the issue product fit, adoption depth, buyer alignment, implementation capacity, or commercial risk?
- How did you explain the decision internally and to the customer?
- What would have changed your decision?

Strong signals:

- Values durable adoption over short-term bookings.
- Can identify false-positive expansion signals.
- Protects trust by declining to sell an unsupported use case.
- Understands that a controlled no can create a better future expansion path.

Decision memo: Customer-growth finalist fit

Date: March 21, 2024
Status: Pre-offer

Decision

Advance CG-A into final references, while keeping the offer gate closed until references and one final Morgan–Devon calibration are complete.

CG-A is the better fit for the customer-growth search as currently defined. This is a choice about alignment with the reset brief—not a conclusion that CG-B is weak.

What the role actually requires

The reset brief calls for a hands-on builder who can:

- Turn Mercury / Evergreen-like design-partner learning into a repeatable adoption and expansion motion.
- Sell and support the product as it exists today, without converting roadmap ideas into customer commitments.
- Work directly with technical buyers, admins, security, procurement, and internal product teams.
- Build lightweight operating discipline without assuming a mature sales organization.
- Separate generalizable product and readiness gaps from one-off customer requests.

Why CG-A fits the current brief

- Repeatable adoption: CG-A has demonstrated the ability to turn messy design-partner learning into reusable milestones, handoffs, and expansion plays.
- Product judgment: She draws a clear line between shipped product, packaging, and later scope. She explicitly understands that selling roadmap as current capability would damage the motion.
- Stage fit: She has operated with founders, limited systems, no SDR layer, and substantial ambiguity—the conditions of the role today.
- Technical-buyer comfort: She can work directly with security, IT, operations, and technical champions rather than depending on a separate solutions organization.
- Operating orientation: Her strongest examples focused on adoption, expansion failure modes, and disciplined learning—not simply quota attainment or marquee logos.

How CG-B compares

CG-B is a capable operator with stronger traditional quota and team-management answers. The concern is fit, not competence.

CG-B appears better suited to a later company moment: a larger pipeline and closing operation, with AE / SE / RevOps support and an organization prepared to absorb a more conventional first-sales-executive mandate. Several answers also leaned toward using future-state vision and executive alignment to move deals before the product was ready.

Choosing CG-B would therefore risk quietly changing the role from “build a repeatable customer-growth motion” to “install a heavier sales machine,” contrary to the reset brief.

Remaining diligence before any offer conversation

References for CG-A should specifically test:

- Pace and urgency in an early-stage environment.
- Willingness to remain the external face while founders are still involved.
- Ability to create enough process without overbuilding.
- Examples of saying no to customer-specific product or roadmap requests.
- Whether her adoption and expansion methods generalized beyond individual design partners.

Recommendation

Proceed with final references for CG-A. If those calls confirm the remaining points above, she should be the leading candidate because she matches the job we said we needed: building repeatable customer growth from real product evidence without making bespoke commitments the operating system.

input.body:
Early-Call Screen Debrief
2024 customer-growth / GTM leader search

Role:
Date:
Interviewers:
Candidates discussed:

Purpose

Compare early-call evidence consistently across the slate. Record observed evidence, not overall hiring decisions.

Search context

The role is intended to turn Mercury / Evergreen-like design-partner and early-enterprise learning into a repeatable customer-growth motion: adoption, activation, expansion, and feedback loops that can be measured and improved. It is not a generic enterprise-sales VP brief, a conventional field-sales build-out mandate, or permission to bend the product around individual prospects.

Rating scale

1 — Limited evidence or meaningful concern
2 — Mixed or incomplete evidence
3 — Solid evidence for this stage
4 — Strong, repeatable evidence
N/O — Not observed

Slate comparison

| Candidate | Enterprise adoption | Product judgment | Early-stage operating ability | Technical-buyer comfort | Stage fit | Evidence confidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

Candidate detail

Candidate:
Current role/company:
Interviewers:
Call date:

1. Repeatable enterprise adoption

What evidence did they provide of creating or expanding enterprise adoption across more than one account, segment, or use case?

- Customer/problem:
- Their specific contribution:
- Adoption or expansion mechanism:
- Evidence of repeatability:
- What was directly observed versus self-reported?
- Rating: 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / N/O
- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

Look for:

- Behavioral milestones, activation, rollout, and expansion evidence rather than logo value or executive enthusiasm.
- A clear account-learning loop that changes qualification, onboarding, enablement, or expansion practice.
- Separation of bounded evidence from proof of broad repeatability.

Watch for:

- Treating one prominent customer, a second department, demos, invitations, or nominal seat growth as automatic expansion proof.
- Inability to explain what changed between the first and subsequent deployments.

2. Judgment about not promising product

How did they handle roadmap boundaries, capability gaps, procurement pressure, or requests they could not responsibly commit to?

- Situation:
- What they said or did:
- Did they distinguish current capability, likely future capability, and unknowns?
- Did they preserve customer momentum without overpromising?
- Rating: 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / N/O
- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

Look for:

- Anchoring the conversation in current product facts.
- Explicit commitments only around actions they control: discovery, documentation, follow-up, or internal review.
- Willingness to pause, narrow, or disqualify an expansion when the product is not a fit.

Watch for:

- Feature dates, bespoke builds, custom implementations, customer-specific pricing or packaging carveouts, procurement concessions, or “we’ll get it on the roadmap” language.
- Treating roadmap ideas as shipped-product evidence.
- Assuming a large logo justifies special handling.

3. Ability to work without a mature sales organization

What did they personally build or operate when process, enablement, positioning, or support systems were incomplete?

- Missing structure or resource:
- Their approach:
- How they prioritized:
- What they created or changed:
- Evidence they can operate independently without creating unnecessary process:
- Rating: 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / N/O
- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

Look for:

- Direct customer learning with a small number of high-fit accounts.
- Lightweight operating discipline: account hypotheses, qualification, stage definitions, activation milestones, expansion criteria, forecast hygiene, and follow-up ownership.
- Ability to sell, onboard, troubleshoot, and synthesize product feedback personally.
- Hiring or tooling that follows evidence of a repeatable motion.

Watch for:

- First answer is to hire a large team or buy tooling.
- Dependence on inbound, brand, marketing-generated pipeline, or founder relationships.
- Importing large-company process before the underlying motion is understood.

4. Technical-buyer comfort

How effectively can they engage technical buyers, understand the underlying workflow, and connect product value to technical and organizational constraints?

- Buyer/persona:
- Technical context:
- Questions they asked or explored:
- How they translated technical detail into a useful commercial conversation:
- Evidence of credibility with technical stakeholders:
- Rating: 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / N/O
- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

Look for:

2024 customer-growth / GTM leader search

Role:

Interviewers:
Candidates discussed:

Purpose

Compare early-call evidence consistently across the slate. Record observed evidence, not overall hiring decisions.

Search context

The role is intended to turn Mercury / Evergreen-like design-partner and early-enterprise learning into a repeatable customer-growth motion: adoption, activation, expansion, and feedback loops that can be measured and improved. It is not a generic enterprise-sales VP brief, a conventional field-sales build-out mandate, or permission to bend the product around individual prospects.

Rating scale

1 — Limited evidence or meaningful concern
2 — Mixed or incomplete evidence
3 — Solid evidence for this stage
4 — Strong, repeatable evidence

- Adoption or expansion mechanism:
- Evidence of repeatability:
- What was directly observed versus self-reported?

- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

- Treating roadmap ideas as shipped-product evidence.
- Assuming a large logo justifies special handling.

3. Ability to work without a mature sales organization

What did they personally build or operate when process, enablement, positioning, or support systems were incomplete?

- Missing structure or resource:
- Their approach:
- How they prioritized:
- What they created or changed:
- Evidence they can operate independently without creating unnecessary process:

- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

- Direct customer learning with a small number of high-fit accounts.

Watch for:

- First answer is to hire a large team or buy tooling.
- Dependence on inbound, brand, marketing-generated pipeline, or founder relationships.
- Importing large-company process before the underlying motion is understood.

4. Technical-buyer comfort

- Buyer/persona:
- Technical context:
- Questions they asked or explored:
- How they translated technical detail into a useful commercial conversation:
- Evidence of credibility with technical stakeholders:
- Rating: 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / N/O
- Confidence: Low / Medium / High

Look for:

- Direct comfort with security, IT, operations, admins, procurement, and technical champions.
- Ability to discuss workflow, rollout sequencing, implementation friction, current product limits, and organizational constraints without hiding behind a solutions team.
- Credible separation of technical facts from later readiness work.

- Ability to build enough process without overbuilding.

results.content:
Recommended posture: conditional approval, not an open-ended “let it run.”

The $300 is small relative to the value of resolving a real enterprise debugging issue, but the query should earn the remaining runtime. This is the same rule we used for the earlier diagnostic logging: preserve useful validation, remove inertia.

Ask Leo by late morning:

1. What exact unresolved question is the query answering?
   - Name the suspected failure mode or support-reproduction hypothesis.
   - Identify what result would confirm or reject it.

2. What evidence is still missing?
   - Why are the normal logs, metrics, or a targeted sample insufficient?
   - Has the reproduction already yielded enough signal to make a decision?

3. What is the minimum viable logging level?
   - Can Leo reduce sampling, narrow it to the affected tenant/request path, or retain only the relevant fields?
   - Are redaction, retention, and access controls still appropriate for enterprise data?

4. What is the stopping condition?
   - A specific artifact, comparison, or reproduction result—not simply “when debugging is done.”
   - Can it be automatically stopped or reviewed at a fixed checkpoint?

Decision rule:

- Keep it running through April 2 only if:
  - the support reproduction remains unresolved;
  - Leo can name the specific evidence still needed;
  - the query is materially better than baseline telemetry for obtaining that evidence; and
  - April 2 is a credible endpoint, with a spend cap of approximately $300 and an interim check-in.

- Taper it today if:
  - the reproduction is complete;
  - the output has not changed the diagnosis or next action;
  - baseline telemetry is sufficient to detect a recurrence; or
  - Leo cannot state what additional evidence the next day of runtime will produce.

- If the evidence is useful but the full query is no longer necessary, reduce it rather than switching abruptly off: targeted sampling, affected enterprise scope only, and standard metrics retained.

My default recommendation, based on the facts you have: approve a tightly scoped continuation only if Leo confirms a live, named diagnostic question. Otherwise taper today. Do not keep a high-volume query running merely because April 2 was the original informal endpoint.

Suggested note to Leo:

“Can you confirm by 11:30 what specific unresolved question the enterprise logging query is answering, what evidence is still missing, and whether baseline or targeted sampling would be sufficient? I’m comfortable carrying a time-boxed query through April 2 if it is still required for the support reproduction, with a roughly $300 cap and an explicit stop condition. If the reproduction is already decision-complete, please taper it today while retaining the baseline telemetry needed to detect a recurrence.”

Suggested reply to Devon:

“Please hold the query as a conditional debugging expense, not a blanket approval. If Leo confirms a live unresolved reproduction and a defined stop condition, we can allow the remaining runtime through April 2 with a roughly $300 cap. If not, Leo should taper it today. Please keep the cost separately identified from the underlying AWS run rate.”

March close language should stay operational and period-accurate:

“March cloud usage remains within the expected operating range, with AWS projected at approximately $19.2k and Pinecone at approximately $4.0k. Neither reflects a contract or prepaid-capacity change. A temporary enterprise logging query associated with a support reproduction may add approximately $300 if it remains active into April; management is time-boxing that diagnostic work and will taper it when the required evidence is complete.”

Keep that in the internal close or operating forecast. Avoid calling it “margin improvement,” “efficiency,” “vendor leverage,” or evidence for financing. The honest H1 message is: monitor recurring usage, distinguish temporary debugging from structural spend, and do not interrupt useful customer-impacting investigation for cosmetic savings.

What the quarterly view can honestly say
- Quarterly cohorts are materially cleaner than weekly cohorts and show better flattening after the onboarding changes.
- Revenue retention improves even after trimming the oversized early expansion customer from the sensitivity read.
- The right external claim is “improving quarterly cohort shape,” not “retention is solved.”

Event-mapping / data-cleanup notes
- I did not use `plan_upgraded` as the expansion source. It still drops or misorders events on retry. Expansion-ready is invoice-backed billed delta plus active-usage threshold.
- `workspace_activated` changed meaning on 2023-03-14. To avoid a fake step-function, I backcasted with the derived 3-core-actions / 2-user rule across the full period.
- `admin_invite_sent` has a backfill gap from 2023-04-04 through 2023-04-07. This affects the admin setup lens, not the core retention curve.
- Self-serve reactivations: if a workspace churned and came back within 21 days, I kept it in the original cohort. If I didn’t, weekly retention would look about 2-3 points better than it really is.
- One oversized early customer still distorts topline NRR if left in raw form. I kept a sensitivity table, but the board version should use the trimmed read or at least footnote the raw.

Caveats / where to attach them
- Weekly operating chart: band shading belongs on the chart itself. Caption should literally say: "weekly cohorts; internal operating signal only; treat only sustained or out-of-band movement as signal."
- Weekly table: keep sample size in the first column. If the n is hidden, people will over-read single-week moves.
- Board slide: no control bands on the main chart. Use quarterly cohorts only. One footnote is enough: "Quarterly first-paid cohorts; latest quarter shown only through available maturity; top-1 expansion outlier trimmed in companion sensitivity view."
- If anyone asks for weekly cohorts on a board slide, my answer is still no. The sample is not stable enough to defend externally.

What I would actually use in the Mercury weekly
- Activation: D14 activated by signup week, with bands, plus the admin setup completion line.
- Expansion: D45 expansion-ready, but only as a directional operating read.
- Admin pain: friction flags per account, because that is where the signal is clearest week to week.
- Do not use W6 retained for the newest cohorts; keep the partial rows visually separated.

Open cleanup before I call this v1
- Finish backfill check on the 2023-04-04 to 2023-04-07 admin invite gap.
- Verify two April workspaces that show invoice deltas without matching seat-change logs.
- Lock one owner for the warehouse pull so we stop proliferating side sheets.

Mark what can power the Mercury weekly, what is safe for the board, and where the control-band / noise caveats belong. I especially want to avoid smuggling weekly wiggle into a board-safe chart.

input.title: Historical analysis brief — retention investigation after the February 13, 2023 lead-partner meeting
input.body:
Historical analysis brief

Subject
What retention investigation Morgan wanted after the February 13, 2023 lead-partner meeting.

Executive finding
Morgan wanted a ground-up reconciliation of the retention story, not another pass at slide design. The investigation was intended to determine whether the apparent retention shape reflected genuine product improvement, customer/cohort segmentation, or faulty measurement across Stripe and application events. The immediate deliverable was a defensible, cohort-by-cohort view that could distinguish logo retention from revenue retention and expose whether expansions or seat adds were masking churn.

Context and trigger
- Before the meeting, Morgan already distrusted the retention slide: Mixpanel and Devon’s CSV disagreed after sandbox and workshop accounts were removed, and the curve became “prettier” too quickly. Morgan suspected the cohort window might be contributing to the discrepancy.
- The February 13 lead-partner meeting exposed the weakness directly. The partner asked two pointed retention questions; Morgan described one answer as hand-waved and the other as only half-answered.
- The usage cohort became especially ambiguous after month 4, when teams moved to annual billing and seat expansion could hide a decline in underlying usage.
- Morgan’s conclusion was that the problem was not label order or deck polish. The number and its construction needed to be investigated.

Investigation Morgan wanted
1. Pull raw cohort cuts
- Stop relying on the blended or hand-shaped presentation view.
- Reconcile the underlying records at the account level, rather than comparing only aggregate outputs.
- Freeze the chart until the definitions and source data were settled.

2. Define the metric precisely
Document, in one place:
- Cohort-entry date.
- Whether the measure is based on revenue, product activity, or both.
- The 30-, 60-, and 90-day windows and the longer month-12 horizon.
- Treatment of immature cohorts.
- Inclusion or exclusion of sandbox and workshop accounts.
- Treatment of expansions, seat adds, reactivations, and other events that could hide churn.
- Exact numerators, denominators, exclusions, caveats, and source systems.

3. Reconcile the competing explanations
The analysis was meant to separate three hypotheses:
- Product improvement: the underlying product behavior and usage cohorts were genuinely improving.
- Segmentation artifact: annual versus monthly plans, team size, customer type, implementation pattern, the 2021 self-serve wave, or other mix changes made the blended curve look better or worse than the underlying cohorts.
- Instrumentation problem: Stripe billing events and application events were missing, misordered, duplicated, or otherwise failing to reconcile with actual workspace activity.

For each hypothesis, Morgan wanted the data to specify what observation would be expected if it were true. If the cuts could not distinguish the explanations, the correct conclusion was that measurement was incomplete—not that retention was healthier than shown.

4. Separate the retention views
Morgan wanted both logo and ARR/revenue retention, with:
- Gross retention shown separately from net retention.
- Expansions and seat adds removed from the gross-retention view so they could not conceal churn.
- Starting and retained logo/ARR counts shown cohort by cohort.
- A clear revenue floor and the definitions underlying each cohort.
- A sensitivity cut excluding the 2021 self-serve wave and other specified mix effects where relevant.
- The eventual month-12 cut presented cohort by cohort, rather than as a blended average.

5. Produce an honest decision-ready output
The intended output was one clean table and a conservative curve or range if the cohort window remained unresolved. Morgan explicitly preferred an unattractive but methodologically clean chart to a polished chart that could not survive a question about its source. The investigation was for answering the partner’s questions plainly, not for manufacturing a better fundraising narrative.

Immediate follow-through recorded in the history
- February 13: Morgan leaned toward pulling raw cohort cuts that night and abandoning further slide polishing.
- February 14: Morgan asked Devon for cohort-by-cohort month-12 logo and ARR retention, starting and retained counts, exact definitions and exclusions, a cut excluding the 2021 self-serve wave, and a view removing expansions from retained ARR.
- February 15: Morgan again requested the real month-12 cut, with expansions and seat adds removed, gross separated from net, and the underlying cohort revenue floor and definitions rather than logo retention alone.
- March 2: Morgan treated the sharper month-12, cohort-by-cohort cut and the version excluding the unusually large early customer as a Q2 deliverable; Devon was to pull raw warehouse data instead of another hand-shaped CSV.
- March 3: The work became a separate retention-cleanup lane owned by Devon with accounting. Morgan wanted the throttled-account-excluded version and stepped out of operating the analysis to avoid shaping the answer.

Historical interpretation
The post-meeting request was therefore an evidence and measurement investigation with three linked aims: establish the true cohort curve, explain the discrepancy between product and billing sources, and determine whether the apparent improvement survived segmentation and expansion adjustments. The recurring principle was to resolve a data gap before revising the story. Later reporting practices—cohort-by-cohort cuts, explicit definitions, separate gross and net retention, and keeping blended/annual views from hiding churn—are continuations of this February investigation rather than a new analytical direction.

Limits of the record
- The available history records the requested investigation and subsequent work assignments, not a single contemporaneous final report that conclusively resolves every hypothesis.
- The February 13 request should not be read as proof that retention was either improving or deteriorating. It was a demand to determine which explanation the data supported.

Source trail
- Morgan Chen, February 12, 2023: distrust of the retention slide; Mixpanel/CSV discrepancy after sandbox and workshop exclusions; possible cohort-window effect.
- Morgan Chen, February 13, 2023: post-meeting diagnosis; month-4 usage-cohort ambiguity; product improvement versus segmentation artifact versus Stripe/app-event instrumentation; planned raw cohort cuts.
- Morgan Chen, February 14–15, 2023: requests for cohort-by-cohort month-12 logo and ARR cuts, definitions, exclusions, gross versus net, and removal of expansions/seat adds.
- Morgan Chen, March 2–3, 2023: Q2 data deliverable and separate Devon/accounting retention-cleanup lane.

Prepared: September 14, 2026

input.title: Historical note — early-April 2023 API v1 billing and inbound-event routes
input.body:
Historical note — not current guidance

Scope: early April 2023.

- On April 6, 2023, API v1 was connected to the new billing setup. The billing routes recorded were `/charges` and `/refunds`.
- Those billing routes used the basic-auth token created the prior sprint.
- On April 8, 2023, the inbound-event route `POST /v1/webhooks` was added.
- The inbound-event route used the same basic-auth setup as the rest of the API; no separate authentication mechanism was introduced for it.

This note records the historical state only. These API v1 routes and basic-auth details should not be treated as current integration or authentication instructions. Later records state that API v1 was retired on April 14, 2023, when the API moved to GraphQL API v2 with JWT authentication.
